He kept his disciples’ letters from being merely formal, insisting that they set down their full states and experiences (ḥālāt o wāridāt) and how they apportioned their time, so that he might know in what occupations their hours were spent and how diligently they discharged their duties. The success of his reforming system, in his view, depended on keeping disciples under full supervision and ordering the whole programme of their solitude and public life (khalwat o jalwat). Hence his refrains: “Be not slack in sending letters — a letter is half a meeting”; “an excuse for a delayed letter, from our side, may be accepted; from yours it is not”; and “the loving letter has not come this long while — my eye is watching for it.” [63] If a deputy failed to report his programme, he would ask directly: “It has not been well made known to me how your precious hours are apportioned — in the company of students, of dervishes, or of neither.” Of one who keeps no discipline of time he writes: “Whoever has no ordering of time is a loser in this world and the next.” And he urges ceaseless engagement: “Be more ardent in your work, so that whoever comes to you takes it up as well.” [64] Sometimes he laid down a timetable himself: in one letter, after detailing an individual round of prayer and supererogatory devotion from dawn until night, he turns to the communal programme — the obligations of the Law to be fulfilled, lessons in Qurʾān-commentary, Hadith, worship, and jurisprudence to be given to the learned between the noon and afternoon prayers, the Ṣaḥīḥ taught after the dawn prayer, and the more advanced led through the Lamaʿāt and Lawāʾiḥ — “for the degrees of stability (tamkīn) are better than the degrees of fluctuation (talwīn).” [65] For personal study he prescribes Hadith and law, ethics and the path — the Iḥyāʾ al-ʿUlūm, the Kīmiyā-yi Saʿādat, the biographies of the early shaykhs — and, in another letter, the Tadhkirat al-Awliyāʾ of ʿAṭṭār, the Nafaḥāt al-Uns of Jāmī, the Manāzil al-Sāʾirīn, and the Rashaḥāt. [66] He watched over relations among his disciples too: when, as humans will, some quarrel arose, he moved to settle it at once and counseled pardon, lest the system be disturbed — “you must on no account take sides against either of these two; rather attend to your own work,” and again, The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 16

Its principles: [68] 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Let the conveying of good (īṣāl-i khayr) be the chief aim — “good” being flight from allother-than-God toward subsistence in God, and the standing-firm of the paths in His love. Let it be done with sincerity and right intention. The thronging of people to one calls for thanksgiving, not avoidance. If gifts come, share them out; the day none come, count it a blessing, “for in poverty and want there is a mighty power.” Do not broach the Unity of Being before all and sundry; weigh a person’s capacity first — “do not publish abroad the question of waḥdat al-wujūd, nor bring it on your tongue before every acquaintance and stranger.” Keep relations with Hindus and Muslims alike, that the non-Muslim be moved by Islam — “the dhikr, by its own property, will draw him toward the community of Islam.” Cultivate courtesy and reverence (adab) among disciples, “for such was the companionship of the prophets with their Companions.” Set them to strive their utmost for the reviving of the sunna and the killing of innovation — “let whoever surpasses his fellows surpass them in this.” He set some of these principles down in his books as well; on the teaching of the invocations, for instance, he directs that “if the disciple is a non-Arab with a ready tongue of his own, let him be instructed in the dhikr in his own language.” [69] Directions for spreading the order He was ever zealous for the order’s spread, commanding again and again: “Strive to propagate the order”; “make every effort that people enter your fold and reach the rank of poverty.” [70] In one letter: “Strive to reform the hearts of the lovers, that they may attain union and nearness; train the seekers in austerity, struggle, love, and self-loss, so that until the Resurrection unbroken openings may come to us and to you.” [71] When Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn asked about accepting gifts, the answer kept the order’s interest foremost: “God has given you both the reason of livelihood and the reason of the hereafter; do that in which the order is furthered. He construes the early Sufis’ acceptance of gifts charitably: “The dervishes of old who took certain gifts did so, most likely, to win the hearts of their devotees; otherwise, for their own need, they would have taken but little.” [73] And when he learns of a disciple’s labour to spread the order, he rejoices and blesses him, holding that the souls of the shaykhs are gladdened by such work more than by any treasure given to their descendants: “May God’s mercy be upon you, that you have set this order flowing — God reward your striving! You have lifted these fallen ones from the pit of heedlessness to the wave of the Presence, and gladdened the souls of the shaykhs.” [74] The khilāfat system From the letters it is clear that Shāh Kalīmullāh built a thoroughly complete and firm system of khilāfat (authorization to initiate and succeed). It was not given to all and sundry, lest, falling into unworthy hands, it spread error. His principles were: (1) the purpose of granting it is struggle for the propagation of Islam; (2) when it is granted, the recipient’s full circumstances are to be reported to the centre, so his fitness can be judged; (3) it is to be given only to the people of knowledge, “so that misguidance will not take hold in his company”; (4) it is of two kinds — the lordly (rabbānī), granted to anyone with the capacity for [spiritual] poverty, learned or unlettered, and that of wayfaring (sulūk), reserved for the people of knowledge; and (5) the authorization is not to be conferred immediately upon a person’s own pledge. [75] When Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn rightly gave khilāfat to one Muḥammad Mīrzā Yār Beg, Shāh Kalīmullāh approved: “You did well — the pearl has been entrusted to a connoisseur of pearls,” adding that from the man’s own letter “the very meaning of love was distilled.” [76] The bayʿa of women Whenever a delicate question arose, Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn sought his master’s guidance — as when the matter of admitting women came up. The reply allowed it, but with safeguards: “Brother, take the bayʿa of women — but hold no long private sittings with young women, which would breed temptation; at the pledge let them rather hold the hem of a garment, hand upon hand, for touching an unrelated woman is unlawful.” [77] By this conditional permission he left women, too, not deprived of inward reform; and when Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn still hesitated, he pressed him: “Why do you hold back from women’s bayʿa? Young or old, fair or plain, treat them all as kinswomen, render them their due, and let the word of truth reach their ears.” [78] Adherence to the Sacred Law He held adherence to the Sharīʿa to be absolutely indispensable for spiritual progress; any striving for advancement apart from it, he was convinced, would prove “a design upon water.” Hence: “One must travel by the road of the Sharīʿa”; and, “Enjoin all who enter the path to adorn the outward with the Sharīʿa and grace the inward with the love of the Lord.” [79] Whoever is not firm-rooted in the Sharīʿa, he taught, is deficient, and his ṭarīqa and ḥaqīqa have no reality: “The [true] man is he who unites in himself Sharīʿa, Ṭarīqa, and Ḥaqīqa.” The Law is the touchstone: “If you would discern the purity of the dervishes, look to a man’s Sharīʿa, for the The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 18

Sharīʿa is the assay by which [spiritual] poverty is made clear.” [80] If a shaykh had ten accomplished disciples, all well-regarded, and one asked which would stand highest on the Day of Resurrection, the answer was: see which is best adorned with the Sharīʿa. And he set out their interrelation: “The minaret of Reality is the Path, and the minaret of the Path is the Sharīʿa; he in whose eye the beauty of the Sharīʿa is greater will find his ṭarīqa and ḥaqīqa the more perfect — the sign of reaching Reality being that, day by day, the wayfarer’s foot grows firmer in the Sharīʿa.” [81] He condemned the “raw” Sufis who had cast off the Law: “These heretics who have let the Sharīʿa slip from their hands — who, for the sake of begging and fat morsels, peddle vapid heretical talk and taunt the Sharīʿa-observant with claims of ‘reality’ — deserve chastisement; their whole profession of [divine] Unity is meaningless, a tepid verbal affair void of [real] state. Beware of sitting in the company of such fools.” [82] The reform of the wealthy When the throng of rich men in Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn’s hospice grew and wearied him, Shāh Kalīmullāh wrote that they too must not be neglected — for in reviving the community no part of society should be passed over: “The purpose of admitting men of wealth is not that they traverse the stations of dervishhood, but that through their joining many others enter the order; for in the common people’s eyes the membership of such men carries great weight.” [83] (Elsewhere: “These are an instrument for turning both elite and commons toward the order.”) So Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn ceased to keep them at a distance and turned to their reform as well. He also warned his disciples about the manner of dealing with kings and nobles: the aim is not to form excessive ties, which disturb the work and obstruct spiritual progress. Acquaintance should be such that, if one must write on a man’s behalf, it be in the manner of Bābā Farīd Ganj-i Shakar: “I have laid this man’s case first before God, and then before you; if you grant him something, the real Giver is God, and if you give nothing, the real Withholder is God — and you are excused.” [86] Flattery and courting kings run against the dervish’s nature: “If kings come to the dervish’s door, it is permissible; but one must not go to theirs”; “the dervish should shun mingling with kings, for consorting with them carries off the lustre of faith.” [87] Samāʿ (spiritual audition) Among the errors of his age against which Shāh Kalīmullāh raised his voice was samāʿ. The Chishtī masters had called it a spiritual nourishment, yet fixed strict conditions without which they held it categorically unlawful — conditions widely flouted in the eighteenth century, scarcely a shaykh observing them fully. So he laments, “Today the shaykhs do not know the worth of [true] samāʿ, nor keep its rules,” and repeatedly bids that it be reduced: “I do not approve of frequent samāʿ; the early shaykhs had no practice of holding it every day.” [88] He directed that its place be taken by murāqaba (contemplation): “Make the circle of murāqaba wider than the circle of samāʿ” — and in most of his letters the direction is to murāqaba. [89] He was not opposed to samāʿ in itself, but the times had made him strict; he kept all its rules himself and bade his disciples, “Hold the assembly of song as we do.” [90] Mindful, too, of the wide influence of the Naqshbandī shaykhs of Sirhind over the kings, he counseled that where their influence was strong the samāʿ assembly be suspended — once writing, when those shaykhs were with the emperor in the Deccan, that it be set aside for the time, “so that the agitation of the opponents may not arise.” [91] His passing (wiṣāl) In his last years he was afflicted with gout and rheumatism of the joints — a hereditary complaint, he notes, of his elders. In a letter written at about seventy-eight he says: “The torment of gout and joint-pain has grown excessive; the left hand, the right knee, and both feet are swollen; for four months I have been bedridden, and can move from room to room only limping, with others’ help; I pray seated, with dry ablution.” [92] Yet even so he strove to the last breath, as his compiler says, “in guiding God’s creatures and exalting His Word,” still writing his necessary directions to Shaykh Niẓām al-Dīn. He passed away on 2 Rabīʿ al-Awwal 1142 AH (17 October 1729), [93] and was buried in the mansion where he had lived, between the Fort and the Jāmiʿ Masjid. A disciple gave the chronogram of his death: “Kalīmullāh was a pure knower of God… I asked the chronogram of his death; Reason answered, ‘He was a Pure Essence’” — yielding 1142. Around his tomb his family long dwelt, and the quarter thrived until 1857, when in the Mutiny the British, on taking Delhi, demolished the houses near the Red Fort. [94] Notes (cont.) 84. Ḥāmid is occupied in the books of wayfaring; Muḥammad Faḍlullāh, aged ten, has memorized twelve juzʾ of the Qurʾān; Muḥammad Iḥsānullāh, aged five, has begun school and is learning his letters. Of the daughters: Bībī Rābiʿa I have married to the house of Muḥammad Hāshim; Bībī Fakhr al-Nisāʾ to a nephew; and the third, Zaynab — Bībī Miṣrī — is fourteen and not yet betrothed.” [95] (Muḥammad Hāshim, who married the eldest, was the cherished son of a religious family of the Deccan who had come to Delhi to study; “since he was exceedingly righteous, a dervish and a dervish’s son, this match was made.”) [96] A grim coda: in a letter to Sayyid Aḥmad Ḥasan Mawdūdī, Ghalib records that by his day Shāh Kalīmullāh’s tomb lay in ruins — “once a fine, populous village… now only jungle, with a grave in an empty field”; the hospice too was demolished in the upheaval of 1857, when the British, on taking Delhi, razed the houses near the Red Fort. PART TWO — THE TREATISE: Kashkūl-i Kalīmī The Kashkūl (“Beggar’s Bowl”) of Shaykh Kalīmullāh Jahānābādī, here translated from the Urdu rendering. The work is built of short sections each titled Luqma (“a morsel”) — the contents with which the bowl is filled. Technical vocabulary is given in transliteration where the exact term matters. The author’s preface In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the All-Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds; and blessing and peace be upon the Master of the Messengers, Muḥammad, and upon his family and all his Companions. This is a kashkūl, a begging-bowl. In it are morsels that are nourishment for the divine subtle faculty (laṭīfa-i rabbāniyya), by which the speaking-soul (nafs-i nāṭiqa) is given strength; morsels that breathe into the frame of merely formal Islam the spirit of true faith, that bring deadened natures into the embrace of everlasting life, and that carry those sick with the cravings of the lower self to the very fountainhead of the All-Merciful’s compassion. These are no dry leaves of a book, but trays heaped with invocations and contemplations (adhkār o afkār) of every kind. These morsels I — the writer of these lines, Kalīmullāh — have begged at the doors of the bountiful and the generous, and gathered for the sake of those whose hunger (that is, whose seeking) is so true that no falsehood taints it. In each morsel of this bowl is a savour reserved for those who carry a particular kind of hunger; none but they are fit for it. From each piece of bread, where one palate will draw delight, another will find nothing but distaste. In short, these many-coloured mouthfuls are the portion of that qalandar who, through the taste of the Path (dhawq-i ṭarīqat), has attained the Reality (ḥaqīqat) that is the true object — content with every fare, plain or rich, so as to give each seeker a share according to his capacity, and let every person of taste savour this bounty to the measure of his longing. Before this, I had prepared a Muraqqaʿ (Album) for the naked-bodied dwellers of the City of Witnessing (shahristān-i shuhūd), that they might clothe their bodies in the garment of Godfearing. Now, at the opening of the month of Dhū al-Qaʿda in the year 1128 AH, at the insistence of certain sincere friends, I gather these begged morsels into this kashkūl, that those who possess taste and longing may take their share, and may aid this lowly one with the light of their minds [and prayers]. We ask of God that we ask of Him nothing but Himself — by the glory of the one whom He chose for the first of the descents and made His elect [the Prophet Muḥammad]. That is: our one petition to God is to ask nothing of Him but Him alone; and we take as our means (wasīla) that noble being whom God selected for the very first descent (awwaliyyat altanazzulāt) and made His chosen one. Preamble (Muqaddima) O seeker of the Real! May God Most High raise you to the loftiest degrees of the knowers. Know this: that Absolute Being (wujūd-i muṭlaq), before it became manifest in the determination (taʿayyun) of created and cosmic existence, was hidden — this Traceless One had no trace. Then, by the demand of that love which It bears for Its own Self, Absolute Being came forth from that pure simplicity, manifested the divine degrees, and descended (tanazzul); and in the station of determination It was called “lover” in respect of the constraint of that determination, and “Beloved” in respect of the exalted determination. Now the perfection of every determination lies just in this: that it turn back toward the Absolute and return into that very colorlessness (bē-rangī) out of which it emerged. The subject of our discourse is, in particular, Man — the comprehensive locus of manifestation (maẓhar-i jāmiʿ) of the Essence and the Attributes, who by reason of “bearing the Trust” stands distinguished among all determinations. His perfection lies in reaching the frontier of annihilation in God (fanāʾ fī Allāh), so as to subsist through subsistence by God (baqāʾ biAllāh). By the First Journey (sayr ilā Allāh) is meant the journey to God, and by the Second (sayr fī Allāh) the journey in God; the utmost of perfection lies in the First, not the Second. Luqma By waṣl is meant cutting off all attachment to other-than-God, withdrawing one’s regard from all created things to be annihilated in colorlessness — that is, in the Absolute. Its forerunner is self-loss (bē-khwudī) and absence from all the senses; the state closely resembles death, the only difference being that in death there is no Presence (ḥuḍūr), whereas here there is nothing but Presence. When the wayfarer reaches this place, sainthood (wilāya) is firmly grounded for him, even if granted but for an instant. If he is then led back into sobriety (ṣaḥw), he is called a possessor of stability (ṣāḥib-i tamkīn); sobriety is sometimes restored at once, sometimes after long delay. But should he remain in that self-loss or intoxication (sukr), he is reckoned among the people of fluctuation (arbāb-i talwīn). The sum of it: in wayfaring, the aim is to be annihilated in the contemplation of the colorless Essence alone. Keep this before your eyes and your wayfaring is whole; let the gaze wander after the unveiling of other determinations, and you stray far from the Straight Path. Luqma In the books of wayfaring such attributes are recorded for every station that, on whichever you cast your eye, you long to halt there alone, and find no rest until you attain it. Yet it is said, “the seeker of the All must die to all.” So you remain caught in perplexity — which station lies before you, and whose practice to set first. In the view of this lowly one, the best course is this: after the obligatory acts, the emphasized sunnas, and the supererogatory sunnas, let the wayfarer persevere with full resolve in the formula of Divine Unity (kalima-i tawḥīd), and give himself to dhikr, fikr, and intimacy (uns). (the luqmas continue) The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 23

…and give himself to dhikr, fikr, and intimacy (uns), remaining firm-footed at his station. For a time he should keep busy amassing a store of supererogatory prayers, recitation of the Qurʾān, tasbīḥ, litanies and offices, and other sources of merit; he must hold aloof from every rhetorical ornament and subtle allusion, and — guarding himself from any outward display of good works — strive night and day to efface his illusory existence (hastī-i mawhūm), until the pull of pre-eternal Self-sufficiency draws him out of his ego-self and brings him to the frontier of annihilation in God, and thence toward the subsistence-of-subsistence (baqāʾ al-baqāʾ). Then the wayfarer will behold the Essence of God, and gaze upon His attributes, traces, and acts. The wayfarer must adopt whatever aids him in this work and avoid whatever obstructs it. This is the way of every practitioner of spiritual exercise, and all the orders agree on it. The seeker of union should therefore take up the exercise (shughl) that frees him from his ego-self; and, as said above, in this nothing surpasses dhikr and fikr. Some kinds of dhikr, however, must be given precedence over others, for the masters established the order thus. Luqma The masters have defined the kinds of dhikr and fikr variously, but the finest statement is alSulamī’s. Dhikr, he says, is of several kinds. One is dhikr of the tongue (lisānī), which is outward. Then there is dhikr of the heart (qalbī) — to cleanse the heart of the cravings of the lower self and the whisperings of Satan, that absorption in God’s remembrance may arise. Beyond it is dhikr of the inmost secret (sirr) — to fill the inner being so wholly that no intruding distraction (khaṭra) can find a way in. And dhikr of the secret is in truth the fruit of dhikr of the heart; the sirr is a subtle faculty (laṭīfa) situated above the heart. Perpetual presence is what the sirr requires, for the heart is in flux at every moment — the very word qalb means “turning” — and through it perpetual presence is impossible. Beyond these is dhikr of the spirit (rūḥ): the annihilation of the invoker from his own attribute, when he sees that it is God Himself who invokes — so neither his dhikr nor state nor attribute remains, for he has known that, before ever he invoked, God was invoking him. Like dhikr, fikr (contemplative reflection) too is of several kinds: to reflect on the sins that issue from one and one’s helplessness in rendering God His due; to ponder the grace God has shown and how deficient one’s thanks are against His bounties; to meditate that all decreed from preeternity is now coming to pass, the Pen having long dried over what is written, so that there remains only felicity or wretchedness; and to reflect on the wonders of the angelic and dominical realms (ʿālam-i malakī o malakūtī), whereby the sense of God’s grandeur is renewed and His promise and threat recalled. Yet, al-Sulamī adds, the one who [merely] reflects has the self for his companion, while the invoker has God for his companion — and on this ground the imams prefer dhikr over fikr. A further proof of that preference: dhikr is an attribute of God, fikr is not; what is His attribute is necessarily perfect, what is not is deficient. The invoker, moreover, turns toward the very Essence, dhikr being the fruit of gnosis and love, whereas the reflective one ponders self, time, state, and number, occupied in self-reckoning. In short, each follows on the other, but dhikr is by far the more perfect and pure — fikr being the forerunner of repentance, dhikr the threshold of arrival at God. As He says, “So remember Me, and I will remember you” — describing Himself by dhikr, not fikr. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 24

Luqma — dhikr of heart, spirit, secret, and the hidden Shaykh ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Jīlī says: the sign of attaining dhikr of the heart is that the invoker hears his dhikr — at all times or now and then, by his capacity — from every thing or from some. The sign of dhikr of the spirit is that he hears the distinct glorifications (tasbīḥāt) of all things, and sees none but God as the true Agent. Aḥmad ibn Ghaylān al-Makkī says: in dhikr of the heart the presence of the Real and the presence of creation stay in balance; in dhikr of the secret (sirr) the presence of the Real prevails, until the invoker has no presence but the Real’s; and the hidden dhikr (khafī) is that one become concealed within the existence of the spirit, as [the cosmos] is concealed within the sirr. Luqma — the aim of dhikr The end of vocal dhikr is this: to make a means of every thing that reminds you of your Object, or to turn toward it — this is the very essence of worship, whether that thing be a name, a rite, an act, bodily or immaterial or other. Conversely, whatever makes you forget the Object — to seek it as a means is sheer misguidance. So all the Sufi’s words, acts, and states are themselves dhikr, provided remembrance, wakefulness, and awareness arise from them; failing that, they are nothing. If I am with You, my profane doings are all prayer; if I am without You, my prayer too is all profane. Luqma Some have enumerated many kinds of dhikr: dhikr of the tongue (aloud or silent); and beyond it, dhikr of the heart (qalb), of the spirit (rūḥ), the hidden (khafī), the more hidden (akhfā), and the most hidden of the hidden (akhfā al-akhfā). Dhikr of the tongue is verbal — having the form of letters, some preceding and some following… (the luqmas continue) …some letters preceding and some following, with account taken of their vowels and pauses. Uttered aloud, this is jahr (vocal); read without voice, it is khafiyya (silent). Dhikr of the heart is the contemplation of the word, or the bringing-present in the heart of a Name’s meaning — drawing the letters of a Name, with their marks, into the heart all at once, without regard to before or after. Dhikr of the spirit forgets word and Name and keeps present only the Named (musammā); in this, invokers differ by their states — for some it comes rarely, for some mostly, for some perpetually, though even these still know “we are invoking, and the One invoked is our Object, present to the eye of insight.” Yet in this too there is a defect: the highest degree is that no trace remains of dhikr or invoker, nothing but the Invoked (madhkūr) — until even the savour of dhikr passes, and one no longer knows of that savour. The stations of the more hidden (akhfā) and most hidden (akhfā al-akhfā) are likewise. Luqma Sharaf al-Dīn Yaḥyā Manērī says dhikr is of four kinds: (1) the tongue invokes but the heart is heedless; (2) tongue and heart both invoke, yet the heart now and then lapses while the tongue stays awake; (3) tongue and heart are wholly accordant, though both occasionally lapse; and (4) the tongue is idle while the heart alone invokes and is present — this is the utmost of the The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 25

stations, for the essence is presence and awareness (ḥuḍūr o āgāhī), which is the very reality of dhikr. At this rank the invoker hears the voice of his own heart, which none but he can hear. Luqma Some masters hold that dhikr befits the beginner, Qurʾān-recitation the intermediate, and supererogatory prayer the one who has arrived. But this humble one submits that on this road the nearest and most uniting course for the seeker is to make dhikr-i khafī (silent dhikr) alone his daily obligation; to cleanse his heart of every imprint; turning from all-other-than-the-Lord, to take up single-pointedness (yaksūʾī); and at every moment to hold to intimacy with the Holy Presence and a firm resolve to be annihilated in it — effacing himself so wholly that no trace of his existence remains. He will thereby miss many supererogatory devotions; but no harm — this is a work that makes good every loss. Luqma — the etiquette of dhikr The Minhāj al-Sālik lists twenty etiquettes: five before the dhikr, eleven during, three after. Before: (1) repentance; (2) keeping the heart at peace; (3) ritual purity; (4) seeking aid (istimdād) from one’s shaykh; (5) knowing that aid sought from the shaykh is aid sought from the Messenger of God, and that from him, aid sought from God Most High. During: (1) sitting cross-legged or kneeling; (2) hands on the thighs; (3) making the place fragrant; (4) wearing clean clothing; (5) keeping the cell dark; (6) covering the eyes; (7) stopping the ears; (8) keeping the form of the shaykh (ṣūrat-i shaykh) present in the heart — the most essential condition of all; (9) holding to sincerity outwardly and inwardly (i.e. not overstating one’s practice); (10) keeping sincere intention (freedom from ostentation); (11) adopting the kalima-i tawḥīd, preferring it over other invocations; (12) keeping the meaning of the kalima present at all times — that every imagined existent is nonexistent, while one stays turned toward the True Existent — negating, at each utterance, every imagined existent. (This, the author adds, like keeping the shaykh’s form present, is most necessary and effective.) After: (1) keeping silence a while; (2) holding the breath; (3) avoiding cold things — cold water or air — lest they chill the heat of the heart. The Minhāj also notes some benefits: the dhikr of the kalima breeds intimacy (uns) in the Holy Presence; if frequent dhikr yields no increase of intimacy, some condition has been neglected, and one should begin anew. Ibn ʿAṭāʾillāh al-Shādhilī says that when a person says “Lā ilāha illā Allāh, Muḥammad rasūl Allāh,” a movement stirs in the Mighty Throne — because the formula belongs to the realm of Omnipotence (jabarūt), ascending toward the dominion (malakūt). [Among the kalima’s recited properties:] reciting it a thousand times each morning in purity eases the means of sustenance (rizq — which, this lowly one notes, may be spiritual as well as bodily); a thousand at sleep sends the spirit beneath the Throne to receive its portion; a thousand at midday drives out a defeated Satan; a thousand on seeing the new moon guards against all illness; a thousand when entering or leaving a city guards from all peril; a thousand with presence of heart, breathed (dam) toward a tyrant, lays the tyrant low; a thousand with the intent that the hidden be disclosed opens the veils of mulk and malakūt; and seventy thousand brings admission to Paradise without reckoning. Luqma — the heart’s becoming an invoker Some knowers say that through dhikr of the tongue the wayfarer reaches dhikr of the heart; so when tongue and heart accord, dhikr attains its perfection in due order — the sequence most orders keep. But the Naqshbandī order is sparing of vocal dhikr, relying on dhikr of the heart together with inward attraction (jadhb-i bāṭin); its beginners start with this very dhikr, and it is said: “Our beginning is the end of every one who [elsewhere] arrives; and our end is that the pocket of desire be emptied” — that no longing remain. What the advanced of other orders attain, the beginner of this one does not; this is simply the Naqshbandī method of training. So there is a difference between the advanced of another order who reach absorption (majdhūb) through dhikr of the heart, and the beginner of this one who attains inward attraction by means of it. Luqma — dhikr of the heart Some jurists deny dhikr of the heart, holding dhikr to be of the tongue only. This is mere cavilling: dhikr is the opposite of forgetting (nisyān), and forgetting is properly an attribute of the heart. This much is certain — that for each kind there are particular rulings that follow upon it. Luqma — the methods of breath-retention (ḥabs-i dam) For some, breath-retention is fundamental to dhikr — indeed, for warding off distractions, “the root of roots.” Among the Chishtī, Kubrawī, Shaṭṭārī, and Qādirī orders it is an indispensable condition; the Naqshbandīs, though not making it a condition, do not deny its value; while the Suhrawardīs make not retaining the breath a condition (so Bahāʾ al-Dīn ʿUmar and Zayn al-Dīn Khwāfī). There are two forms: ḥabs-i dam (retention) and ḥaṣr-i dam (confinement). Retention is itself of two kinds — takhliya (emptying) and tamliya (filling). In takhliya one draws the breath up from the belly, pulling the navel and its surroundings toward the back, and holds it — in the chest, some say, or in the brain. There is no need to press the fingers on the nostrils, eyes, or ears (though some do so for precaution); its proper method is to perform it submerged in a pool — the method Khiḍr taught ʿAbd al-Khāliq Ghijdawānī, from which great effect is hoped. In tamliya one draws the breath into the belly, expands it, and holds — driving the navel far back; this generates much heat and digests food well. Confinement (ḥaṣr-i dam) is to take in somewhat less breath than usual, cutting it off in both directions; it too heats the heart, though less than retention. All this, however, concerns the travelling breath (dam-i musāfir). The resident breath (dam-i muqīm) is free of heat and cold, needs no changing, and never departs: whether one retains or confines, the resident breath persists in every state. Whoever knows it and makes it the measure of every dhikr becomes one who invokes perpetually (dāʾim al-dhikr); the chain of presence accords with him, lengthening as far as he wills. During the days of retention, avoid sour and very moist foods. At first, blood may come from ears, nose, or stool — no cause for alarm; keep at the work and it soon passes. Avoid very hot food (heat being innate or accidental), lest disease arise. Increase the duration gradually, never to the point that the practice becomes oppressive; release the breath slowly and through the The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 27

nose — never the mouth, which can harm the teeth. Most important: in retaining, the stomach should be neither full nor empty but in a middle state — though this counsel is for beginners; one perfected may hold or release at will. The masters took these methods from the yogis (jogīs); the fit hold to them with great regularity. Luqma Some people of gnosis say: when a person’s self cleanses the inward (tanqiya-i bāṭin) and, emptied of all craving for sense-objects and familiar things, is filled with absorption in dhikr (istighrāq-i dhikr) and the gift of presence, a relation (nisbat) with the spiritual realm arises in him, and by it his heart is illumined. He then beholds, by that light, the Essence of God, and through the divine ordinances comes to know what God wills. The light then passes from his insight (baṣīrat) into his outward sight (baṣārat), so that he apprehends the unseen world with his outward organs — and at that point he departs from this world both outwardly and inwardly. Luqma — praiseworthy and blameworthy bewilderment Among the stations the first is repentance, and the last is bewilderment (ḥayrat) — though some make contentment and surrender (riḍā o taslīm) the last, in its place. Bewilderment is of two kinds: blameworthy (madhmūma) and praiseworthy (mamdūḥa). The beauty and perfection of God’s Essence demand bewilderment, not doubt. The two are sometimes confused, but the bewilderment of the Essence arises from the gnosis and apprehension of a thing, whereas doubt is the fruit of ignorance and unfamiliarity. Bewilderment occurs in presence (ḥuḍūr), doubt in absence (ghaybat): the bewildered one ascends moment by moment toward the heights and reaches the innermost reality (kunh) of the thing, drawn by longing to apprehend it; the doubter falls with equal speed into the lowness of ignorance, having no interest in knowing the thing’s reality. Bewilderment, it is said, is compounded of two elements: a cognitive one — knowledge of the thing’s existence — and an ignorant one — unawareness of its innermost reality (kunh). Doubt wavers between the two, securing neither: the doubter’s knowledge is of doubtful existence, his ignorance of doubtful establishment, and he circles forever between negation and affirmation. This is the doubt named blameworthy bewilderment; its opposite is praiseworthy bewilderment. The blameworthy is the portion of the common folk, whereas …praiseworthy bewilderment is the lot of the elect. Luqma — the Lights (anwār) The lights that appear are sometimes white, sometimes green, sometimes like carnelian, and last of all black — this black light being the light of the realm of Omnipotence (jabarūt). Their discernment: a light joined to the right shoulder is an admonition, the light of the right-hand recording angel; not joined to the shoulder, it is the light of the pīr (shaykh); appearing from in front, it is the light of the Messenger of God. A light on the left, joined to the left shoulder, is the left-hand recording angel’s; not joined, it is a satanic deception — as is any form that appears from the left. A light from above or behind is the guardian angels’. A light that comes with no awe, breeding fear, after which no presence remains, is likewise a satanic deception. But if The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 28

presence is sustained at the light’s appearing, and separation and longing (firāq o ishtiyāq) arise at its passing, it is surely the Light of the Sought (nūr-i maṭlūb). A light above the chest or navel is satanic deception; above the heart, it is from the heart’s purity. In every case, the sincere seeker should neither rest content in, nor exult over, any of these lights. Luqma — the perpetuity of contemplative vision (dawām-i mushāhada) Whether mushāhada is perpetual for the knower is disputed — one group affirms it, another denies its permanence. A knower says: “The contemplation of the righteous is between disclosure and veiling.” The truth is that, once the bond of the heart (rabṭ-i qalb) and the connection of the inmost secret (ittiṣāl-i sirr) become firm and realized, arrival (wuṣūl) never lapses — though the lights and unveilings (anwār o mukāshafāt) come and go. This is the sense of the Sufi saying, “al-waqt sayfun qāṭiʿun wa barqun lāmiʿun” — the [spiritual] moment is a cutting sword and a flashing lightning. Luqma — the utmost of gnosis (nihāyat-i ʿirfān) In absence and self-loss, absorption and annihilation, there is a state beyond words: at that time there is nothing but the Oneness (aḥadiyya) of God and Absolute Being. Should someone object that Absolute Being cannot enter apprehension — since whatever is apprehended is contingent (ḥādith), while Absolute Being is pre-eternal (qadīm), and the pre-eternal cannot come within our grasp — we say he speaks rightly; but the point is that, in the state of annihilation, the wayfarer forgets the relation that would require affirming both an ascribed and a thing-ascribed-to, and becomes wholly heedless of and suspended from it. This is the annihilation of annihilation (fanāʾ-i fanāʾ). Here there is non-apprehension (ʿadam-i idrāk), not the apprehension of non-existence (idrāk-i ʿadam). As Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq said: “Incapacity to attain apprehension is itself apprehension” (al-ʿajzu ʿan darki l-idrāki idrāk). If it be asked what the Sufis’ terms mean — shuhūd, tajallī, maḥabbat, and maʿrifat of the Essence — and how they are realized: it is a fruit of gnosis to set each thing in its rank and give it its due. In our matter there are two things: the Essence as pure simple Essence in itself, and all that is other than the Essence. The first’s due is affirmation, the second’s is negation; in the first, gnosis’s due is that [the Essence] not be known [in its kunh], in the second, that the thing be known as it is. So affirming the Real as Real and the false as false is equally gnosis; and from not knowing a thing it does not follow that it does not exist. Hence the holy Essence is affirmed, realized, yet unknown (muthbat, muḥaqqaq, ghayr-maʿrūf). Thus witnessing the Essence means the Essence’s absence from these [created] matters; tajallī of the Essence, that these matters become hidden from insight; love of the Essence, that love is cut off from these matters; gnosis of the Essence, that familiarity with them no longer remains — and so for every term ascribed to the Essence. So the gnosis of the Real is only in His Names, Attributes, and Acts, and even there bounded to the surface, not the kunh; for the road to the kunh of any thing is closed, the kunh of each thing being the Reality of the Real, which no human, angel, or jinn can apprehend. Reality, then, is never apprehended in full — this is the rank of all-encompassing gnosis (ʿirfāni basīṭ). Well has it been said: “The beginning of the common folk is the end of the elect; and the start of [the vision of] Beauty is the terminus of the learned.” Yet — “See the difference of the road, from where to where it runs!” The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 29

Luqma — the shaykh’s spiritual aspiration (himmat-i shaykh) All this ordering of exercises, invocations, and contemplations is merely conventional terminology; but the ordering that pertains to himmat (the shaykh’s spiritual aspiration) does not depend on it. Here the shaykh accomplishes the disciple’s “emptying” (takhliya) along the lines of the Law; and whether the disciple be absent or present, the shaykh’s aid reaches him through himmat. It is by the shaykh’s himmat that the doors of [divine] effusions (fuyūḍāt) open upon the disciple… This path, however, is very rare; mostly it is the capricious who seek it, unable to do the Path’s works and shrinking from its hardships, so they crave an easy way. Luqma — the need for a shaykh (ḍarūrat-i shaykh) It is said: “Whoever has no shaykh, his shaykh is Satan.” So every person of heart must seek a shaykh. But a difficulty arises: being himself a beginner, the seeker cannot tell reformer (muṣliḥ) from corrupter (mufsid), saint from non-saint, and may err either way. Shaykh Sharaf al-Dīn Yaḥyā Manērī resolves it thus: the divine custom runs so that no age is ever empty of shaykhs, ascetics, devotees, the awtād, nujabāʾ, nuqabāʾ, abdāl, aqṭāb, the Ghawth, and all the people of God. So the sincere seeker must attend regularly upon the shaykhs known to walk this path, go again and again to their assemblies, and each time probe his own heart — seeing whether the crowd of whisperings and distractions overlaying it is dispelled, whether in some assembly he feels release from the heart’s turmoil, or it stays as before. If he feels such release, and this gift has come to him from that elder’s door, let him make that elder’s company (ṣuḥbat) binding on himself — for if a little company gave this, much more is hoped from constant company. But if he feels no change at all, let him understand his portion is not with this shaykh, and — without letting denial enter his heart — seek his remedy at another door. Luqma — the prayer for finding a perfect shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī says: whoever rises at midnight, makes ablution, prays two rakʿats with as much Qurʾān as he can, then prostrates and implores God with great earnestness and weeping, reciting the prayer below — God will open upon him the door of arrival and bring him to one of His saints to guide him toward Himself. This prayer, much tried, is: “O my Lord, guide me to one of Your servants brought near, that he may guide me to You and appoint for me the road of arrival to You.” The later Shādhilī masters add that whoever, always with presence of heart and without fail, keeps reciting the durūd sharīf and the kalima “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” will surely find a perfect shaykh (shaykh-i kāmil); in this path, they say, their exemplar is Imam Ḥasan [ibn ʿAlī alShādhilī]. THE FIRST WAṢL (Waṣl-i Awwal) The Invocations (Adhkār) May God grant you success in what pleases Him and wherewith He is content. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 30

The initiation. When a sincere seeker comes to a perfect shaykh to acquire the method, the shaykh should bid him keep three consecutive fasts (or, if he cannot, break each with a little food), reciting daily a thousand times “Lā ilāha illā Allāh,” “Astaghfiru llāh,” and the durūd. On the third night, bathed and present before the shaykh, let him recite the Fātiḥa, the Ikhlāṣ, “Āmana al-rasūl” (Q 2:285–6), the istighfār, and “Shahida Llāh” (Q 3:18) to “ḥakīm.” Then the shaykh says: “You have pledged allegiance to me, weak as I am, and to my shaykh, and to the shaykhs of my shaykh, and to the Messenger of God, and to the Lord of Glory; and you have covenanted to keep your limbs obedient to the Law and to devote your heart to the love of God.” He places his hand on the disciple’s right hand — in accord with the verse “The hand of God is above their hands” (Q 48:10). Those seated around take hold of the seeker’s hem, each linking to the next, so that all present form one connected chain. The disciple then affirms his pledge; the shaykh invests him with the mantle (khirqa), saying “That is the garment of God-fearing, and that is better” (Q 7:26); and in private instructs him (talqīn) in whatever dhikr suits his state, unknown to any other. Sub-section. The method of instruction: the shaykh utters the dhikr once and the disciple listens; the disciple utters it and the shaykh listens; thrice so; then the shaykh “commits it over” — “as it reached me from my great elders, so I convey it to you” — and the disciple accepts. Then he is ordered: after each prayer, ten durūd and ten Ikhlāṣ; the six rakʿats of Awwābīn with three salāms; two rakʿats with intent of “preserving faith” (method in the Muraqqaʿ); a hundred “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” before sleep; and the Fātiḥa recited for the order’s shaykhs. Sub-section. The adhkār are given precedence over the murāqabāt; some, though, begin with murāqaba, and if the disciple’s capacity demands it, that too is allowed — the more effort, the better. But the preferable course is to “colour” the seeker first with dhikr, kindling fervour, then by murāqaba make him “colourless,” replacing fervour with stillness. The adhkār themselves differ greatly: for a disciple overly drawn to the world, begin with nafy-o-ithbāt (negation-andaffirmation); for one with the scent of love in him, teach the Name of Majesty, “Allāh”; for one whose nature holds tenderness and a leaning toward worldly detachment and release (iṭlāq), instruct him in “Hū” (He). Each person has a separate course; one must weigh every case. (It is not our aim to record the thousands of adhkār and murāqabāt in other books, but only those with the rank of kernel that the great Sufis specially chose — for whoever holds the higher degrees holds the lower too.) Luqma — posture and the kindling of the heart For seclusion, choose a narrow, dark place and sit cross-legged. Though such sitting is ordinarily reckoned an innovation and the seat of the proud, in dhikr it is permitted, for the Prophet, after the dawn prayer, would sit thus engaged in dhikr until sunrise. Keep the back perfectly straight, eyes closed, both hands on the knees. With the big toe of the right foot and its neighbour, grip firmly the vein of the left foot, so heat is generated in the heart — by which the heart is cleansed, the fat around it (said to be the dwelling of the “whisperer,” khannās) melting, and the whisperings and “wind” thereby lessened. Then, one in heart and tongue, engage in dhikr — aloud, soft, or as the moment requires — observing the conditions of the verse: The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 31

The isthmus (barzakh) of the Essence, the Attributes, the lengthening, the doubling, the below and the above — displays to the lovers the whole of selves, the above and the longing. Here: by barzakh is meant the form of the shaykh; by Essence, the Absolute Being of God; by Attributes, the seven perfect attributes (Life, Knowledge, Will, Power, Hearing, Sight, Speech). Madd (lengthening): drawing out “Lā ilāha.” Shadd (doubling): the tashdīd of “illā Allāh.” Taḥt (below): beginning “Lā” from the end of the left knee and carrying “ilāha” up to the right shoulder, pausing there to settle the breath. Then, with full force, striking “illā Allāh” upon the heart — this is fawq (the above). Luqma — intrusive thoughts (khaṭarāt) Intrusions are of four kinds: (1) satanic (shayṭānī) — breeding pride, anger, enmity, envy; (2) egoic (nafsānī) — breeding craving for food, lust, greed, hoarding, adornment; (3) angelic (malakī) — prompting worship, obedience, meritorious acts; (4) merciful (raḥmānī) — breeding sincerity, love, longing. The end of the left knee is the place to repel the satanic (the left being Satan’s seat); the end of the right knee, the egoic (Satan and the self being ever in league in temptation); the right shoulder, the angelic (the recording angel’s seat); and the space of the heart is the touchstone of the merciful and the place to fix it firmly. If the wayfarer neglects these distinctions, disturbance and disorder may enter his state. So instruct him in a comprehensive formula, by stages: first “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” (no god but God); then “Lā maʿbūda illā Allāh” (none worshipped but God); then “Lā maqṣūda illā Allāh” (nothing aimedat but God); then “Lā maṭlūba illā Allāh” (nothing sought but God); then “Lā mawjūda illā Allāh” (nothing existent but God) — by which all intrusions are repelled. In this lowly one’s view it is best to begin with “Lā mawjūda illā Allāh,” for the shorter and lighter the journey, the better. And if the disciple is a non-Arab, instruct him in the dhikr in his own tongue. Luqma — the two-stroke dhikr (dū-ḍarbī) Its one stroke, “Lā ilāha,” is struck upon the right shoulder; its other, “illā Allāh,” upon the space of the heart — delivered in succession. After “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” three, five, seven, or nine times, one says “Muḥammadun rasūl Allāh” once. Being simpler than the four-stroke dhikr, it carries less dispersion (tafriqa). Luqma — the order of dhikr After negation-and-affirmation comes affirmation, and after affirmation the Name of the Essence (ism-i dhāt). One should say “Allāh” more than “illā Allāh,” and “illā Allāh” more than “Lā ilāha illā Allāh.” Luqma — the dhikr of laqlaqa In this dhikr, the word “Allāh” is said continuously, without break, and softly. In it one may keep the mouth open or closed — both are correct; some retain the breath in it, some do not. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 32

Luqma — the three-footed dhikr (sih-pāya) This dhikr resembles a three-footed ewer (ibrīq): if any one foot is missing, it cannot stand. So this dhikr has three pillars: (1) the Name of the Essence (ism-i dhāt, “Allāh”); (2) the regarding of the seven attributes; (3) the intermediary (wāsiṭa), also called barzakh. Its seven conditions are named in the verse — barzakh (the intermediary/the shaykh’s form), Essence (“Allāh”), Attributes (the “mothers” — Knowledge, Hearing, Sight), shadd (fully pronouncing the tashdīd of “Allāh”), madd (prolonging its alif), taḥt (beginning the hamza forcefully from below the navel), and fawq (carrying it up into the brain and ending it there). These seven generate in the seeker, at every breath, a fresh taste and longing. Luqma — the ascent and descent (the attributes-dhikr) Since this dhikr is never done without breath-retention, retention was not listed separately in the verse. Method: draw the hamza of “Allāh” up with full force from below the navel; hold the whole breath in the chest; say “Allāh” in the heart, and with it “Samīʿ” (All-Hearing), picturing its meaning; likewise “Allāh” with “Baṣīr” (All-Seeing); then with “ʿAlīm” (All-Knowing) — this is the ascent (ʿurūj). Then reverse: “ʿAlīm,” “Baṣīr,” “Samīʿ” — the descent (nuzūl). Then again “Samīʿ,” “Baṣīr,” “ʿAlīm” — the second ascent. The secret: the compass of “Samīʿ” is narrower than “Baṣīr,” and “Baṣīr” narrower than “ʿAlīm.” The wayfarer begins in the rank of reason and witnessing (ʿaql o shahādat) — the narrowest — so he puts “Samīʿ” first; advancing to the rank of the unseen (martaba-i ghayb), wider, he puts “Baṣīr” first; passing into the unseen of the unseen (ghayb al-ghayb), wider still, he pictures “ʿAlīm,” then returns. (Order: Samīʿ–Baṣīr–ʿAlīm ascending, ʿAlīm–Baṣīr–Samīʿ descending, Samīʿ–Baṣīr–ʿAlīm again — one dhikr, two ascents about one descent.) The retention should let the wayfarer perform this up to two hundred and fifty times in a breath, until a heat arises that burns the inward “fats” — the dwelling of the whisper-stirring khannās — so that distractions are checked and absorption prevails. Taḥt holds many benefits but countless straits; the dhikr is deficient without it, so it cannot be avoided — yet the invoker should perform it without excessive distress, asking God for protection. In full: sitting cross-legged, gripping the kaymās vein of the left foot firmly with the right toes, drawing the navel in and slightly up, eyes closed, the shaykh’s form present in the heart, draw “Allāh” up intensely from below the navel, prolong its second lām, and regard “Samīʿ,” “Baṣīr,” “ʿAlīm.” When one can utter “Allāh” with the three Names 250 times in a single breath, add five further attributes — Dāʾim (Permanent), Qāʾim (Subsistent), Ḥāḍir (Present), Nāẓir (Watching), Shāhid (Witnessing); when these too reach 250 per breath and one partakes of each one’s lights, add seven more (the “Seven Imams”); and when steadfastness is gained, go on to the compound attributes — e.g. Akram al-akramīn, Arḥam al-rāḥimīn, Ajwad alajwadīn, Dhū al-faḍl al-ʿaẓīm, Rabb al-ʿarsh al-ʿaẓīm. Luqma — the dhikr of the Shaṭṭārī order Per the Shaṭṭārī rule, say the Name of the Essence with the tongue or in the heart, fixing the Names of attributes — “Samīʿ,” “Baṣīr,” “ʿAlīm” — in the mind; then, keeping the barzakh (the shaykh) before the eye, draw [the breath] from below the navel so that the dhikr reaches the palate. In the lesser striving (muḥāraba ṣaghīr) do this once per breath; in the greater striving (muḥāraba kabīr), a hundred times per breath. Observe ascent and descent; in the greater The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 33

striving retain the breath with full force, fixing the shaykh’s form, until one passes into self-loss and unconsciousness. The Object that is hard to grasp even with much wakeful forgetting is, by this dhikr, attained in a short while. Luqma — the six-stroke and four-stroke dhikr This dhikr of “Allāh” is called six-stroke (shash-ḍarbī) and four-stroke (chahār-ḍarbī). The sixstroke: strike one blow in each of the six directions. The four-stroke: sitting facing the qibla, place before you a muṣḥaf (Qurʾān) or the grave of a saint; strike the first blow to the left, the second to the right, the third upon the muṣḥaf or grave, and the fourth upon the heart. By this, absorption in dhikr is attained, and the meanings of the Qurʾān or the states of those in the graves may be disclosed — but here picturing the shaykh’s form is essential, or there will be no benefit. Luqma — the Ḥaddādī dhikr Begin “Lā ilāha,” with prolongation and the shaykh’s form, from the left side; let it stand on both knees; then strike “illā Allāh,” with full intensity, upon the space of the heart, having sat [for it] — striking the dhikr so that, as one would knead with both hands, it is driven home with full force into the whole body. So continue until taste (dhawq) begins to come. This dhikr is transmitted from Abū al-Ḥafṣ al-Ḥaddād, and there is much exertion in it. Luqma — breath-watching (pās-i anfās) [the dhikr “Lā ilāha illā Allāh”] Bring “Lā ilāha” out with the outgoing breath and draw “illā Allāh” up with the breath — keeping dhikr with the breath’s coming and going, the gaze ever fixed (open or closed) upon the navel. Do this dhikr so much that the invoker’s dhikr runs on even while asleep. By it, the invoker’s life is, as it were, doubled. Luqma — breath-watching (pās-i anfās) [the dhikr “Allāh”] Sometimes breath-watching is done with the word “Allāh”: utter the “A-” of “Allāh” as the breath comes — a “wāw” arises in it, [read as] “Hū” — and when drawing the breath in, utter “Allāh” with the breath; so that the breath becomes, as it were, the tongue of the heart; and when the breath is released, “Hū” is uttered with it. In breath-watching one may use “Allāh” or “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” — both are equal. If, while doing it, a sound issues from the nostrils, this is called “the nose’s drone” (irra-i nāk); it breeds much agitation and burning, with heat and dryness in the brain, so the nose should be anointed with almond oil and the head massaged with it. This dhikr must be brought to perfection — and perfection is that the breathing keeps invoking even without the invoker’s consciousness or will. Luqma — the heart-to-heart dhikr (sīna ba-sīna) For a person on whose heart-tablet no imprint of dhikr or fikr has yet formed: the master seats him directly opposite, knee touching knee — the disciple’s chin on his own chest, the back curved inward, the chest thrust out, both eyes closed. The shaykh then attends to the disciple’s breathing: when the disciple draws breath in, the shaykh releases his own onto it; when the disciple breathes out, the shaykh draws in. Doing so, an agitation suddenly arises in the disciple, and the dhikr of “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” or of “Allāh” (whichever rules in the master’s The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 34

station) begins to flow from the disciple’s tongue and breath. So overpowering is it that, from its heat, blood may flow from the disciple’s nose and ears. It is called “heart-to-heart” because its instruction is given without the tongue’s mediation. (But if the disciple is already engaged in a practice — especially murāqaba with breath-retention — this device will not work, since he has already retained his breath; indeed the master’s own self-loss may so affect the disciple that he is suspended from his own thought — such a thing once befell the author in an assembly with his pīr, reversing the very state of the gathering.) Luqma — the dhikr for unveiling the spirit (kashf al-rūḥ) Whatever the spirit, wherever it be, by this dhikr it is made present. First say “Yā Rūḥ al-Rūḥ” (O Spirit of the spirit) twenty-one times, striking upon the heart; then, raising the head, say “Yā Rūḥa mā athnā Allāh.” When finished, turn toward the Object, and in sleep or waking that spirit becomes present; said two thousand times, the Object is very soon attained. Sayyid Gēsū Darāz learned this from Khwāja Naṣīr al-Dīn Maḥmūd Chirāgh-i Dihlī. Luqma — the abbreviation of the kalima dhikr Some abbreviate the kalima ṭayyiba to “Ha, Hu, Hi,” striking the first blow right, the second left, the third upon the heart. Luqma — the dhikr for unveiling the graves (kashf al-qubūr) Sitting by a grave, face raised to the sky, say “Iktashif lī yā Hū” (Unveil for me, O He), striking upon the heart; then say “Iktashif lī,” striking upon the grave opposite the dead one’s face, and “…ʿan ḥālihi” (concerning his state). By this, the dead person’s state becomes known, openly or in a dream. Luqma — the dhikr for the answering of prayers (ijābat al-daʿawāt) Saying “Yā Rabb,” strike upon the right armpit; “Yā Rabb,” the left armpit; “Yā Rabb,” the heart; ending with “Yā Rabbī.” Do this in abundance; when about to finish, raise both hands, say “Yā Rabbī,” pass the hands over the face, and keep one’s object present in the heart. This is transmitted from the Shaykh of Reality, Ibn ʿArabī. Luqma — the method of dhikr in the Naqshbandī order Pressing the tongue to the palate, retain the breath; begin “Lā” from the navel and carry it up to the brain; incline “ilāha” toward the right shoulder, and thence, saying “illā Allāh,” go to the left and strike the space of the heart so forcefully that its effect appears through the whole body. Drawn as a figure, the path runs navel → right shoulder → brain → heart (a V-shaped tracing of the kalima across the body). This figure is that of the word “Lā”; conforming to it, make yourself nothing and affirm the Real, saying with the heart’s tongue: “My God, You are my object, and Your good pleasure is my sought” (Ilāhī anta maqṣūdī wa riḍāka maṭlūbī). No outward motion should be felt; keep it even with the breath-retention, and when ending the retention say in the heart “Muḥammadun rasūl Allāh.” Its effect: by the negation the invoker is himself negated, by the affirmation affirmed. If the count passes twenty-one with no effect, no absorption, begin again — surely some condition was faltered in; else this dhikr never fails to show its effect. Luqma — negation and affirmation (nafy o ithbāt) Begin it — two-stroke or four-stroke — picturing, on the right, the Prophet; on the left, one’s own shaykh; and before the heart, God Most High. (Some picture, directly between the two sides, the Presence of Absolute Being.) Luqma — a dhikr for repelling illness Say “Yā Aḥad” (O One) to the right, “Yā Ṣamad” (O Eternal Refuge) to the left, and “Yā Witr” (O Unique) upon the heart. Luqma — [another] dhikr for answered prayers After the ʿishāʾ prayer and its supererogatory, say “Yā Wahhāb” (O Bestower) seventy times — worldly needs are met; then pray two rakʿats, reciting after the Fātiḥa the Ikhlāṣ eleven times in each. Luqma — dhikr while walking Walking fast, say at each step “illā Allāh, illā Allāh.” Walking slowly, say “Lā” raising the right foot, “ilāha” raising the left, then “illā” on the right, “Allāh” on the left. At a middling pace, say “Allāh, Allāh” at each step. Luqma — the dhikr of the four realms The whole formula “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” is the dhikr of the human realm (nāsūt); “illā Allāh,” of the dominical (malakūt); “Allāh,” of the omnipotent (jabarūt); and “Hū,” of the divine realm (lāhūt). (the heart-to-heart transmitted invocations continue) These are instructed to disciples only in their later state, once they have passed through austerities, strivings, and the forty-day retreats (chilla-kashī) and attained complete purification. Each in detail: The dhikr of “withness” (maʿiyyat). When the witnessing of Essence and Attributes is deficient, one is taught “Yā Maʿī, Yā Maʿī; Yā Hū; Yā Hū, Yā Hū” (O You who are with me; O He). Sit as in the prayer’s qaʿda, the buttocks on the ground, feet out; grip the left arm with the right hand and the right arm with the left, firmly; and utter the words with five strokes — first between right foot and right knee; second toward the sky; third between left foot and left knee; fourth upon the liver; fifth upon the heart, with full force — bearing in mind that “Hū” means the Absolute Oneness, which has no like. In these days take milk (saffron mixed in is better still) and use perfumes freely. (Sometimes it is reduced to “Hū, Hū, Yā Maʿī,” the first struck skyward, the last upon the heart.) The dhikr of the All (kulliyya). “Bika l-kull, minka l-kull, ilayka l-kull, yā kulla l-kull” (Through You the All, from You the All, to You the All, O All of the all) — and, in one version, “Allāhumma anta l-kull, wa minka l-kull, wa bika l-kull, wa laka l-kull, wa ilayka l-kull, wa kullu l-kull.” The dhikr of encompassment (iḥāṭa). “Yā Muḥīṭu ẓahran wa baṭnan” (O Encompasser, outwardly and inwardly) — at “ẓahran” open the eyes, at “baṭnan” close them. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 36

The dhikr of effacing the directions (maḥw al-jihāt). “Anta fawqī… taḥtī… amāmī… khalfī… yamīnī… shamālī… anta fiyya, wa anā maʿa l-jihāti fīka; aynamā tuwallū fa-thamma wajhu Llāh” (You above me, below, before, behind, on my right, on my left, within me; and I with all the directions am in You — wherever you turn, there is God’s Face, Q 2:115). Stand facing the Throne for “above”; sit looking down for “below”; face forward, behind, right, left in turn; strike the heart at “within me”; then rise and turn round for the close. The dhikr of the self-disclosure of “I-ness” (tajallī-i anāniyyat). After tahajjud, a hundred times “Innī anā Llāhu, lā ilāha illā anā” (cf. Q 20:14): head raised skyward for “Innī anā Llāhu,” turned right for “Lā ilāha,” then a forceful strike on the heart for “illā anā.” (In these five, picturing the meanings and picturing the intermediary are a condition.) Bābā Farīd Ganj-i Shakar’s Punjabi dhikr: Uhawl tūñ (pointing to the higher realms), Ihawl tūñ (the lower realms), Tūhīñ tūñ (absolute release). When the assembly ends, say thrice “Subḥāna Llāhi wa bi-ḥamdihi, subḥāna Llāhi l-ʿaẓīm,” then the prayer: “O God, You said, ‘Remember Me and I will remember you,’ and I have remembered You by the slightness of my knowledge, reason, and understanding; so remember me by the amplitude of Your Self, bounty, knowledge, and forgiveness. O God, open the ears of our hearts to Your remembrance, O Best of those remembered.” THE SECOND WAṢL (Waṣl-i Duwwum) The Contemplations (Murāqabāt) Murāqaba means so to guard the heart that nothing other-than-God can ever enter it. The heart’s disease of “being occupied with other-than-the-Real” has three causes: the self’s chatter (ḥadīth-i nafs) — which comes by purpose and volition, in solitude or company; the intrusive thought (khaṭra) — which comes and goes without intent; and looking-towardother (naẓar ba-ghayr) — the knowledge of the multiple things. The true cure is to keep the inner being occupied with the Real; and inward occupation is of several kinds. In place of the self’s chatter, establish the Supreme Name (ism-i aʿẓam, the Name of the Essence); in place of the intrusion, set the Names of the attributes (the “mothers” — Life, Knowledge, Will, Power, Hearing, Sight, Speech); and fix the heart’s gaze on the beauty of the master (jamāl-i murshid) — this being what is called the link, bond, and intermediary (wāsiṭa, rābiṭa, barzakh). Luqma — Annihilation (fanāʾ) “Regarding the holy meaning” means regarding the Name of the Essence in one’s mind, free of any fixed phrasing or lexical sense, while attention rests wholly on the pine-cone-shaped heart (qalb-i ṣanawbarī) — for which a luminous mind and retentive nature are needed. If the wayfarer cannot fix this meaning, let him picture it as pure light, and himself effaced and dispersed within it — as if the light were a sea breaking on the shore and he a single drop within it; or let him picture it as pure darkness (utter blackness), and himself a shadow — for when a shadow enters the darkness it is effaced, no distinction remaining between shadow and dark. Luqma — the subtle faculty of the heart (laṭīfa-i qalbī) Some knowers describe the exercise thus: the disciple brings the form of his pīr and shaykh present in his imagination, until the heat and condition particular to the people of the exercise arise, and its effects …begin to appear in the disciple’s being. Now, with the condition gained from picturing the shaykh’s form, let the disciple turn toward his own comprehensive human reality (ḥaqīqati jāmiʿa-i insāniyya) — making it the form of the shaykh and regarding it as his shaykh-inreality. But since this comprehensive reality — technically the “heart” (qalb) — cannot indwell bodies, bringing it present is difficult; so let the disciple turn toward his pine-cone-shaped heart (qalb-i ṣanawbarī), the “lump of flesh” (muḍgha), with an attention that makes all his senses single-pointed — for the real heart has a bond with the figurative heart that it has with no other member. In this state, indifference and self-loss come over the disciple: he should take this as a straight road (rāh-i mustaqīm) with no crookedness in it, picturing himself walking it — and that road is endless. Luqma — deliverance from intrusive thoughts If an intrusion pursues the wayfarer and he flees it, either it falls behind and gives up the chase, or it overtakes him. To be rid of it: turn toward the comprehensive reality found in the master’s form, and hold that state as long as possible. If that fails, “empty the brain” (takhliya-i dimāgh) — expel the breath forcefully through the nose — and turn again to that reality. If that fails, recite abundantly: “Astaghfiru Llāh… min jamīʿi mā kariha Llāh, qawlan wa fiʿlan… wa lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā bi-Llāhi l-ʿaliyyi l-ʿaẓīm” (with full accord of heart and tongue). If that fails, take up the Name “Yā Faʿʿāl” (O Doer of all He wills), holding its sense in mind — it has a special property against whisperings. If that fails, ponder the meaning of “Lā ilāha illā Allāh” as “Lā mawjūda illā Allāh.” And if that fails, with full prolongation and aloud, say “Allāh” and strike a blow upon the pine-cone heart. Luqma — the station of bewilderment (maqām-i ḥayrat) Whatever comes within the five outward and inward senses is either true (accords with reality) or false (does not). For those who hold the Unity of Being (waḥdat al-wujūd), it is established that, like the true, the false too is among God’s manifestations. So Abū Madyan al-Maghribī — Ibn ʿArabī’s master — says: “Deny not the false in its modes, for it too is one of His manifestations; and give it its measure from yourself, until you render in full the due of its affirmation.” And al-Jandī adds: “The Real indeed appears in its form, while the ignorant, in its very essence, deny it.” Therefore, in all universals and particulars that come to the self, contemplate Absolute Being appearing under a particular determination — the finest method for barring intrusions. By it, all-other vanishes, a savoury state is attained, and the cosmic and divine ranks begin to be perceived. Better still, negate even “contemplation,” make the unseen condition firm, abandon the self, and grasp self-loss and unconsciousness firmly — for to the realized of this road, coming out of absence (ghaybat) is tantamount to unbelief, even when the aim is reflection on realities; because absence and self-loss carry the wayfarer toward that valley named bewilderment — and bewilderment is the final station.
