Luqma — the union of union (jamʿ al-jamʿ) With the eye of the heart, behold your own reality (the “comprehensive reality”), and in all states and acts keep it before the heart’s gaze. Then in all existents — beautiful or ugly, subtle or gross, sensible or not — you will see your comprehensive reality flowing and pervading, until you attain the vision that all the worlds subsist through it and it permeates all existents — they becoming for you like mirrors in which you regard it. Or: all the worlds become as a single body, and the wayfarer as its spirit. This rank is jamʿ al-jamʿ. When this murāqaba grows strong, the wayfarer becomes aware of all that befalls the worlds, joy or sorrow — for the spirit must be apprised of its body’s pain and ease. [A supporting practice:] Write “Lā ilāha illā Allāh,” or simply “Allāh,” on a paper and keep it before the eyes; or, with the inward eye, contemplate that imprint on the tablet of the imagination. Keep the attention fixed on this written figure of the kalima until indifference comes and the figure is wholly forgotten — until one no longer even knows it has been forgotten. Luqma — self-loss (bē-khwudī) Fix the eyes unblinking upon some stone, clod, grave, muṣḥaf, flower, or upon the face of the shaykh or the beloved, or some other thing; and direct the inward faculties too toward the Absolute, unqualified Reality (ḥaqīqat-i muṭlaqa-i ghayr-i mukayyifa — free of all qualification and quantification) — until the avenues of intrusion close, the marks of overpowering self-loss and absence come over one, and the seeker becomes oblivious of everything, to the point of being unaware even of his own obliviousness. This [self-loss] method is ascribed to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham. Luqma — the most complete focusing (atamm al-tawajjuhāt) Some masters describe “total focusing” (tawajjuh-i tāmm) on the Presence of the Real thus: O seeker! When all your faculties — outward and inward, partial and total — are suspended from their own operations, and your heart is emptied of every cognition, belief, and all-other-thanGod, then turn toward God and know Him as He truly is — confining Him neither in bare transcendence (tanzīh) nor in anthropomorphism (tashbīh). Let this focusing be undifferentiated and formless (ijmālī o hayūlānī), such as accepts all forms — good and bad, sensible and not — with utter affirmation of [His] Unity, with resolve, recollectedness, and sincerity. Keep this state ever-standing, never falling into scattered thought or weak intent. Hold firm that God’s perfection encompasses all attributes, whether or not their excellences come within our grasp; and know that neither reason, reflection, nor fancy can draw near the curtain of His secrets. He is just as He is: if He wills, He shines forth in one form, or in all the forms of all the worlds; and if He wills, He stays transcendent and pure of them all. It is fitting that, from the beginning of the ranks of self-disclosure to their end, the wayfarer regard only [the one Being as their locus], making this his constant aim — seeing nothing but one Absolute Being (wujūd-i muṭlaq): conditioned being and Real Being, though outwardly two, are as Being one and the same, release and conditioning being mere relations. Perseverance in this regarding yields a boundless savour. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 39

Short methods. (a) Close both eyes, fix the gaze on the heart, and know God present, watching, and with you. (b) Keep both eyes open and fix the gaze upward or forward, unblinking; from this, lights appear, and from the eyelid a fire blazes that spreads through the body and births [divine] love (ʿishq). (c) The sultan of invocations (sulṭān al-adhkār): keep both eyes open and fix the gaze on the tip of the nose so that the black of the eyes vanishes and only the white shows, until recollectedness is gained and intrusions wholly cease; this is called “the praiseworthy station” (maqām-i maḥmūda) — one may sit as in prayer or in the “dog-sitting” posture, and fixing the gaze on the eyebrows yields many benefits. Luqma — a comprehensive yogic seat Yoga has eighty-four postures (āsana), each with its own benefit; but Shaykh Bahāʾ al-Dīn Qādirī chose one seat comprehending all: sit cross-legged, feet together, the left heel beneath the testicles and the right foot beside it, contract the anus, draw the breath up and gather the navel toward the back, close the mouth and press the tongue to the palate; then occupy yourself in the breath, reflecting inwardly “He alone is” (Ū hī hai) — staying hungry and forgoing sleep. Kept up three continuous days without food or sleep, such self-loss comes that the veils of the unseen open and unveiling (mukāshafa) begins; then one either returns to sense or remains rapt (majdhūb). If not attained in three days, repeat for three more — but in each interval eat, drink, and sleep a little, lest melancholic madness (sawdāʾī) be feared. Luqma — the ascent of the spirit (the fikr the masters conceal) Sit as in prayer and regard “ʿAlīm,” “Samīʿ,” “Baṣīr” together with the shaykh’s form. When steadfast, incline the face toward the heart, close the eyes, gaze on the heart with the inward eye, and picture that you behold God. When steadfast in that, sit so but raise the gaze skyward, eyes half-open, and picture that your spirit has left the body and, passing beyond the heavens, is occupied in the beholding (dīdār) of God. To one steadfast in this, a green thread appears — one end above the seventh heaven, the other in his heart. This is the highest degree of fikr, the very exercise the masters conceal; in it, the “intermediary” (the shaykh’s form) is not used. (Transmitted by Chirāgh-i Dihlī from Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ.) Luqma — a murāqaba of Gēsū Darāz Stay still and think, “I am not; He alone is”: “I am not, and the friends witness God; I am not; soul of my soul, secret of my secret — I am not.” Reflecting thus, the verse comes as command: “The truth has come and falsehood has vanished” (Q 17:81), and the voice of “I am You” (anā anta) is heard — the nearest of all roads. Luqma — the dhikr of “Allāh” Whoever stays occupied in murāqaba and the dhikr of “Allāh,” upon him the self-disclosure of the whole cosmos dawns. Bāyazīd (Sulṭān al-ʿĀrifīn) kept this from childhood to death. Luqma — the contemplation of the ascension of the knowers (miʿrāj al-ʿārifīn) Suppose all existents to be mirrors; take every perfection your reason or senses find in them to be forms of God’s Names and Attributes. Suppose the whole cosmos one mirror, and see God in it with all His Names and Attributes — and you become of the people of vision (ahl-i The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 40

mushāhada). Then press further: looking at the cosmos, know that your own essence encompasses the universe, all of it imprinted within you, your essence the mirror of all — so contemplate God now within yourself. Then further: regard the possibles, as they are, as nonexistent; bring them not into the middle, but take all as forms of God’s self-disclosures, subsisting through Him — so all this perfection and beauty is God’s, and it is in God Himself that you contemplate it. Then higher still: remove your own existence from the middle, so that the contemplator and apprehender is none but God — He alone is then the Witness and the Witnessed. Luqma — wayfaring in the Naqshbandī order Naqshbandī wayfaring rests on three methods. First, focusing and murāqaba (tawajjuh): to turn toward that Meaning — without “how,” without “of-what-sort,” without likeness or model — which is understood by the Name “Allāh” (the Essence that has no like or peer). Second, the bond (rābiṭa): to turn toward the form of the shaykh (annihilated in God, subsisting through God) until absence and self-loss arise and that form — far lowlier than the goal — vanishes from view, while the gaze falls on the sea of witnessing and Essence and on the Presence of God (the highest direction). Third, the silent dhikr (dhikr-i khafī) of “Lā ilāha illā Allāh,” which comprehends negation and affirmation. Of these, the first is best and highest, but hard to attain until it works its effect within; the second, the rābiṭa, is the nearest, and through it wonders manifest; the third is the firmest, its foundation most solid. Luqma — mirror-gazing and picturing the Name Gaze often into a mirror, fixing the shaykh’s form in the imagination, keeping the gaze ever on it, until your own form vanishes from the senses. And: write “Allāh” in gold or silver ink and gaze on it always; imprint the imagined form of the word “Allāh” on the page of the heart and keep the attention turned to it, until absence from the senses is attained. Conclusion (Khātima) O seeker of the Real! May God make the end of your works good. Know that perseverance (mudāwamat) in any single one of the kinds of dhikr and fikr set out in the two Waṣls will bring you to the Sought. Without perseverance, absorption, and total engagement, to dream of union (waṣl) is proof of folly — for Sufism is to be practised, not spoken; the more you train, the more you attain. As Abū al-Ḥafṣ al-Ḥaddād said, “Sufism is nothing but a slow cooking to ripeness.” When these notions ripen and reach the marrow of the soul, strange and wondrous contemplations come to elite and common alike — delight to the one who has the station, amazement to onlookers. But some fools who learn a few invocations call themselves Sufis on that alone; it is God’s boundless forbearance that bears their sins, else they would surely destroy themselves. Others prove even less — flailing briefly for show, then, feeling no savour, abandoning the work for worldly affairs; or, content with that little, laying snares of fraud …take a whole world to ruin, fancying themselves knowers — all profitless: what gain is there in raising a corrupt building on a corrupt site? May God preserve us from such ranks. The true man sets foot manfully on this road and renders the Path its due; and until he becomes a possessor of real effect (ṣāḥib-i taʾthīr), let him breathe no word of it to anyone. This much is warning enough; beyond it, all is in God’s hands. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 41

[This Khātima] consists of a particular method of dhikr, for the disciple of independent discernment (ṣāḥib-i ijtihād) whose outward is already adorned with capacities of every kind. I have strong hope that, keeping to this order, he will rise from the lowness of dispersion (farq) to the height of union (jamʿ). Success is in God’s hands, and to bring one to the Sought is His work alone; at every moment our reliance is on Him. Luqma — simple and compound knowledge (ʿilm-i basīṭ o murakkab) Knowledge is of two kinds. If the “known” is one in every respect, its knowledge is simple (basīṭ); if the known is multiple but apprehended undifferentiatedly (ijmālī), this too is simple — though the first is “really simple” (basīṭ-i ḥaqīqī), the second “virtually simple” (basīṭ-i ḥukmī). But if the known is apprehended through several differentiated (tafṣīlī) aspects, that is compound knowledge (murakkab). The lofty aspiration of the Sufis is ever bent on dissolving compound knowledges to reach the simple knowledge of the Necessary Being — that this recollectedness (jamʿiyyat) be theirs always, or at least mostly; and, fleeing the dispersion that the thought of all-other breeds in the heart, to take refuge in that recollectedness. The vanishing of all-other is fanāʾ fī Allāh; the vanishing even from this sense of presence is fanāʾ-i fanāʾ. Luqma — hearing the heart’s “Allāh” Let the seeker sit alone in a corner, in full purity, facing the qibla, eyes closed, tongue pressed to the palate. Turning to his heart, let him think: “the piece of flesh in my breast (the heart) is saying ‘Allāh,’ but I do not hear it.” Let him strive to hear it, bending his whole himmat upon it. With God’s help, soon a movement will be felt — which he may suppose to be of the heart, or the self, or mere whispering. Then let him strive harder still that it grow clearer, until no confusion with the self’s movement or with whispering remains, and he knows for certain (bi’ltaḥqīq) that this movement is the heart’s lump of flesh, saying “Allāh, Allāh.” Likewise. This is a state in which the heart becomes an invoker; it falls to each by his rank — some quickly, some only after long effort. But the seeker should not despair, for it is said: “Despair not of God’s mercy; none despairs of it save the unbelieving folk” (Q 12:87). Breath-retention. If the breath’s coming and going keeps the heart-movement from appearing, hold the breath below the navel; then the heart becomes like a vessel sheltered from the wind, its water perfectly still — hold until the movement is felt. But not so long as to risk a fatal illness, for that harm outweighs the good; do only as much as you can, releasing the breath slowly, mindful here too of the heart’s movement. Luqma — guarding the heart’s movement (nigāhdāsht) When the heart’s movement is sensed and its dhikr runs, guard it well, for it is so faint that the least resistance drives it away — and then striving only diminishes it. Do not despair: seek the lost wealth with humility and brokenness (ʿajz, inkisār, khushūʿ, khuḍūʿ). Usually it is the self’s chatter, an intrusion, or the knowledge of the multiple things that slips the thread from the hand — as set out at the start of the Second Waṣl; for the heart to be essentially turned two ways at once is impossible. Likewise. When this lofty gift comes, reckon it no trifle, but stay night and day tending this relation (nisbat). Only in utmost need turn to another task; if even supererogatory prayers, litanies, or Qurʾān-recitation interfere, set them aside — though if they do not disturb the relation, there is no harm, and they become aids. Stay wholly in the relation until, opening the eye a little, you can keep turned to the heart even with eyes open. This is “solitude within the crowd” (khalwat dar anjuman). When, by divine support, this relation grows strong, then even if the wayfarer should at times forget, he recovers it by attention — and on recovery it grows ever greater, no longer driven off by any hindrance; and at this rank he gains great delight and recollectedness from the dhikr. Luqma — the dhikr spreading through the body When the heart’s movement reaches the point that the tongue feels no trouble at hearing “Allāh” from the heart, the movement that arose from the pine-cone heart spreads through the whole body — first appearing in some one member (a hand, a foot, the head will move, though the seeker does not intend it). But the condition is that he never turn his attention to the member’s movement, for that makes the heart heedless; his whole attention must stay on the heart alone — in this work the heart is head and chief, all members its followers. Likewise. When the dhikr’s light spreads, it soon encompasses the whole body, from head to the nails of the feet, every member filled with dhikr. Then varied states come over the wayfarer — now laughing, now weeping; now joyful, now sad; now amazed, now ablaze. Whatever the state, pay it no heed; keep only to the dhikr. The most important point: if divine support attends, “Allāh” is heard from the whole body at once, all members chorusing with the heart. Sometimes the predominance of dhikr (ghalaba-i dhikr) is greater in some members, less in others; sometimes equal in all — and the greatest delight is when it is equal in all members, a condition the Sufis term the sultan of dhikr (sulṭān al-dhikr). Luqma — the heart’s dhikr becoming audible Knowledge of the heart’s dhikr comes at first without the faculty of hearing; but once it settles firmly, most begin to hear it with the ears too, and for one of sound nature the “curtain of the intermediary of audition” (wāsiṭa-i istimāʿ) clears of itself. But the common notion that another person can hear the wayfarer’s heart-dhikr — from near or far, by the differing ranks of hearers — is a popular error. As Manērī notes in the Maʿdin al-Maʿānī: if some have reported hearing such a sound from certain practitioners, the reason may be that, drawing the dhikr up from the breast, a faint sound issues from the throat, which the hearer supposes to be the heart’s — though it is not. “We have ourselves seen and heard such a sound produced; for the rest, God knows best.” Luqma — the overwhelming of savour (ghalaba-i dhawq) Sometimes a particular savour (dhawq) gained from the appearing of some thing overwhelms the wayfarer — a hindrance to his advance. If his inner faculties are troubled by it, let him keep fully to the outward and inward etiquettes and turn to his shaykh; if the shaykh understands his state and knows the cure, let him tell it plainly or by hint, and if not, hold it in suspense, [saying] the time for its unveiling has not yet come. Luqma — the aim of dhikr The aim of dhikr is to become annihilated in the Invoked (madhkūr). So do not content yourself with merely pronouncing the Name of Majesty with tongue and heart — though even that yields some benefit; for without the presence of the Invoked, the pearl of the goal is not gained. The aim is annihilation in the Invoked, not in the Name of the Invoked. Luqma — the overwhelming of dhikr (ghalaba-i dhikr) Among the wondrous visitations of this rank, one is that the wayfarer becomes aware that all created things perform dhikr. Coming gradually, it should not be halted at, for the goal lies far beyond. A subtle point: at this rank, engrossed in the dhikr of “Allāh,” people hear the forest, desert, doors, walls, stones, pebbles — or, leaning on something, their own hands and feet — saying “Allāh, Allāh.” In truth the cause is the predominance of one’s own dhikr over oneself — wholly distinct from actually hearing the universe’s dhikr; for every creature has its own “dhikr of state” (dhikr-i ḥālī), as most hold (some affirm a “dhikr of speech,” maqālī), and awareness of each creature’s glorification (tasbīḥ) requires fully apprehending their differing meanings. Each individual of the universe is marked by a different dhikr, each species having its appointed one. Yet if, in the state of the dhikr of “Allāh,” the wayfarer hears a particular dhikr of the wall, the door, the prayer-mat, and so on, it may be the dhikr of those things, of which he is apprised — though at this rank room for the other possibility remains. Luqma — continuous movement (ḥarakat-i muttaṣil) After this lofty rank, sometimes, in total attention on the pine-cone heart, a movement is felt in the heart and the subtle head-centres, unlike the former in quality — for the first was disjoined (munfaṣil), this is continuous (muttaṣil). The first resembled the unbroken repetition of “Hū, Hū”; the second, “Hū” uttered once with a long prolongation. Or: the first is like water falling from place to place, the sounds distinct yet successive; the second, the sound of a waterfall, falling unbroken. Or: the first is like a hammer’s repeated blows; the second like one stroke on a bronze vessel, lingering long — loud at first, then dwindling to faintness. The second is far subtler, felt only after much training. The first (disjoined) movement the wayfarer can refer to the word “Allāh,” “Ḥaqq,” or “Hū” — each having a sonic shape with beginning and end. But the second, so continuous and single that neither beginning nor end can be traced, cannot be referred to those discrete words; rather, refer it not to the dhikr but to the Invoked — not the Name but the Named. (In the first, the Named is attained only incidentally; in the second, the Named is what is essentially regarded — so the masters teach.) If it be objected that the goal is so absolute that we cannot predicate of it even “absoluteness” as a limitation (neither lā bi-sharṭ shayʾ nor lā bi-sharṭ lā shayʾ), and so how can a sensed movement be referred to it — the answer is that what has more absoluteness is nearer the goal, and the second movement, having more absoluteness than the first, is more like it. In reality both movements are from the world of descents (ʿālam-i tanazzulāt) and among the manifestations of the Names and Attributes; this road to the goal appears when the wayfarer steps from fanāʾ toward baqāʾ. At the beginning of my [spiritual] state, seeking the straight path, I came to an elder (Muḥammad Ṣādiq, khalīfa of Miyāñ Pīr Muḥammad Sāwan). My exercise then pertained to fikr, yet I felt a thirst. He said the exercise fitting for me was the eternal sound (ṣawt-i The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 44

sarmadī, also ṣawt-i lā-yazālī; in yoga, anhad — “limitless,” since it has no beginning or end). He taught it: stop both ears with the index fingers and attend single-pointedly; a sound is heard, like water falling continuously. Keep the attention fixed on it, never heedless; when firm, loosen the fingers and attend, so that the world’s noise does not stop it — increasing the practice until it is heard without stopping the ears, prevailing over all sounds, yielding a savour beyond tongue or pen. (Some wrap a peppercorn in cotton, or red silk, in the ear, whose heat strengthens the sound — and after a year such peppercorns become good for eye-diseases.) I practised it and found unprecedented delight; but I asked when I would reach the goal, since this longing, though real, could not equal it. He said Miyāñ Mīr of Lahore and his disciples did this very exercise and called this sound “the Presence of the Real.” Being then a student of formal knowledge with the standard books before me, and a beginner, this distressed me, and I abandoned the exercise. Later, granted [the journey] to Medina, I told the story to my shaykh, Yaḥyā Madanī, who said: “This exercise is very beneficial, and is shared between the possessors of miracle-grace (aṣḥāb-i karāmat) and the people of [satanic] gradual-luring (ahl-i istidrāj). Its effect is to remove scatteredness and produce recollectedness, making one single-pointed — a means of connection between the seeker and his goal; and it produces the self-loss and absence that are the prelude to fanāʾ al-fanāʾ. As for calling it ‘the Real’ — that is by the resemblance to the language of absoluteness implicit in it; otherwise the Real’s majesty is: ‘There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing’ (Q 42:11).” Luqma — the annihilation of annihilation (fanāʾ al-fanāʾ) When the continuous movement begins to be felt, it spreads through the whole body in some (by purity of temperament and strength of the movement) and stays confined to one part in others; either way, its appearing turns the wayfarer toward the goal. If attention toward the goal does not arise, let him attend to the heart’s lump of flesh, without regard to any Name; if that is hard, attend by way of a Name — but at this degree there is great peril in attending to the bare Name without the Named, indeed [stopping there] is “unbelief” by comparison: “the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near” (ḥasanāt al-abrār sayyiʾāt almuqarrabīn) expresses just this. The wayfarer’s knowledge of this movement should itself be, as it were, a movement coinciding with it — for knowledge alone has “magnitude” (miqdār), and all these exercises serve its growth, since reward and rebuke, nearness and distance, presence and absence all rest on knowledge. Since the root of every movement is the heart, draw the knowledge of this movement from the heart alone, not from another member (which only draws attention to the [other] bodily members). When the whole body is ennobled by this movement — every fibre filled with dhikr — then [refer] the Invoked to this movement of the whole body …[refer] the Invoked to this movement of the whole body, and refer the knowledge to this Invoked. So three things coincide: (1) the movement of the whole body; (2) the Invoked (the meaning of “Allāh,” in reality the Named, musammā); and (3) the knowledge of the Invoked — their coinciding being like that of distance, speed, and time (a problem of mathematics, met in the discussion of accidents under the questions of quality). At this rank the throng of absence and self-loss presses in: this is the stage of fanāʾ al-fanāʾ. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 45

Luqma — knowledge of the Invoked without the heart’s mediation When, by austerity, the wayfarer mostly retains the knowledge of this “movement,” he should now spend his aspiration on attaining it without the mediation of the heart’s lump of flesh, his attention in no way toward it — until his attention is cut from the movement of the lump of flesh or the whole body, and only the knowledge of the Invoked remains; with both sides (or one) becoming non-existent, the coinciding too lapses. Nurture this relation with full aspiration, from fewness to abundance to permanence. If, through weakness of the relation, it cannot be held without the movement, again make the movement a means; and if even the “wholly disjoined bodily movement” is lost, turn to the “partial disjoined cardiac movement”; and if that too goes, then — if possible — bathe in cold water, or expel the breath forcefully two or three times (takhliya), or repeat the Name “Faʿʿāl” several times with presence of heart and grasp of its meaning. God willing, the lost thing returns. Luqma — the presence of the Invoked (ḥuḍūr-i madhkūr) When divine favour attends and, by austerity, the presence of the Invoked (God) is retained even without the whole-body movement, let the wayfarer never be heedless of this great wealth for a moment — whether occupied in the acts of the body or of the heart, his state should be: Take in hand, O brother, the end of the thread of this wealth; pass not this precious life in heedlessness. Always, everywhere, with everyone, in every task, keep, in secret, the eye of your heart turned toward the Friend. Luqma — the cardiac dhikr (dhikr-i qalbī) If attention to the Invoked comes without the coinciding [of movement], reckon it a very great wealth, for here the cardiac dhikr is gained — impossible while “movement” stands in the middle. The heart (dil) is a merciful subtle faculty (laṭīfa-i raḥmānī): some say it is neither body nor bodily; some call it the “apprehending faculty”; some “immaterial,” some a “subtle vapour,” some from the “world of the Command,” some an accident, some a substance — and some keep silence. (We have detailed this in our ʿAshara-i Kāmila, with the applications of qalb, nafs, rūḥ, ʿaql — and that the movement seen in physical bodies is stages removed from the heart.) Luqma — the appearance of lights (ẓuhūr-i anwār) As the cardiac dhikr nears, lights begin to appear — within (in the heart, the head, the right or left hand) or without (from the right, the left, the head, or directly in front); all these forms are good. Rarely they fill the whole body. But to halt at this rank, enamoured of the lights, profits nothing: the wayfaring of one to whom no lights appear is safer from peril and likelier to reach the goal sooner. Though the lights are a mercy, strive rather that the [pure] knowledge arise — without direction — so the relation between knowledge and the Known be one of absoluteness. The wayfarer finds in his heart a relation like a thread (ḍorī) running from his heart toward the Essence of the Sought — but it ends short, for that Essence, by its absoluteness, is free of being joined by any thread; perforce the thread, bound to the Absolute Affair, becomes so undetermined that no trace of quality or quantity (kayf o kamm) remains. Those without the rational sciences waver at this; those versed in them are untroubled. The “flatness” (bē-mazgī) the beginner feels — reckoning this binding a kind of idleness — has no cure but to make ʿishq The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 46

his helper, bring his utmost ardour to bear, and, mindful of the lofty ranks that are its reward, ready himself; once his conception ripens, he will know what treasures lie in it. The masters here forbid excess litanies and supererogatory prayers — anything that might sever this relation. When attaining the Absolute Affair proves hard, some bid the disciple turn to the whole cosmos without regard to any determination, for once determination is removed, only formless absoluteness remains. Some picture the Absolute Essence as a boundless sea of light, themselves a drop merged and lost in it; some, as boundless darkness, themselves its shadow lost within it; some, as a void between earth and sky. All are likenings of the intelligible to the sensible for the weak of reason — for how far is that Most-High Essence from such likenesses! The aim of all is that the wayfarer’s illusory existence (hastī-i mawhūm) — which veils his eyes from the vision of Absolute Being, his own reality — be annihilated. When, by the overpowering of state, he retains no knowledge of his self, nor even of his knowledge, fanāʾ is attained; and when not even the knowledge of that knowledge remains, that is fanāʾ-i fanāʾ. “The more I go out from myself, the more I come into Your embrace.” The upshot: the wayfarer finds within himself a relation but knows not where its other end is bound. Whatever he binds it to will have a determination (taʿayyun), and the Sought (majestic His station) is beyond it — indeed beyond whatever rank he halts at, for whatever enters his conception is a determinate thing his mind encompasses, and what is bound by any limit can never be the Sought. Hence it is said: no prophet or saint has reached the kunh of the Absolute. “The ʿAnqā is no one’s prey — take up your net; here the net catches nothing but wind.” So let the wayfarer understand: “I am turned toward Him, but know not in which direction I am turned” — he knows, but knows not what he knows: this is fanāʾ. And if he knows, knows not what he knows, and knows not even that he knows: this is fanāʾ-i fanāʾ, the final rank of the journey to God (sayr ilā Allāh) — beyond which begins the journey in God (sayr fī Allāh). Luqma — the two kinds of annihilation Annihilation is of two kinds: the first when the wayfarer has compound knowledge (ʿilm-i murakkab), the second when his knowledge becomes simple (basīṭ). By compound knowledge is meant the condition of apprehension that arises within, cut off from all-other, awaiting only the Presence of the Object — because whatever enters the wayfarer’s apprehension is apprehended not under the attribute of otherness (ghayriyyat) but [under] identity (ʿayniyyat) …[finds in it] identity (ʿayniyyat), to the point that the garb of the [divine] affairs and determinations in which a thing is clothed has, in his view, no external existence, and he reckons this apprehension real and conformable to fact — as the proponents of the Unity of Being (waḥdat al-wujūd) have explained at length. Or else the cause is his utmost attention to the Object and excess of love, so that by the intensity of ʿishq whatever enters his apprehension appears as the Object alone, and other-than-Him does not come into view. Yet in reality it is not so: these are in fact multiple, various existences belonging to the particular existence of the Necessary Being, which by his utmost ardour appear to him thus — and “all is He” (hama ōst) is not conformable to fact but false; the proponents of waḥdat al-wujūd have [merely] cooked a raw notion. Be that as it may, both parties agree on effacing the “other” as other; so the wayfarer, fleeing the multiple sciences, takes refuge in the single knowledge and thereby attains nearness to God. Still, he knows that he knows — and on this ground his knowledge is “compound”: a knowledge whose relation is toward another knowledge. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 47

So long as your self-conceit (pindār) remains in you, know for certain you are still mired in idol-worship. As for simple knowledge: the wayfarer turns toward his goal so wholly cut off from all-other that not even this knowledge remains (that his knowledge has been severed in its relation). Here his knowledge is said to have become simple, and he has attained real annihilation (fanāʾ-i ḥaqīqī). (Some call compound knowledge fanāʾ, and simple knowledge fanāʾ-i fanāʾ.) These ranks are not [won by effort] but are bestowed (wahbī), their effusion from God’s court — the wayfaring of wayfarers has neither effect nor part in them. “One must not [merely] seek, that the Object should come; rather the Object must will that one should seek.” Luqma — attraction and sainthood (jadhb / wilāyat) This [annihilation] is the utmost rank of attraction (jadhb), self-loss, and longing, falling to some fortunate one; it has signs, and not every claimant can claim it. Until the wayfarer attains the rank of attraction, he cannot enter the ranks of sainthood (wilāyat): without it he may be among the ascetics, the devout, the good and righteous — but he does not reach the “nearness of arrival” (qurb-i wuṣūl), also called sainthood. Know that jadhb is, by careful view, a condition for sainthood, but its being perpetual is not: some remain for years in attraction and intoxication (sukr), then come to sobriety (ṣaḥw) — of Bāyazīd it is said he remained thirty years in this station — and some are drawn (majdhūb) for but an hour. Those majdhūbīn who became bound at this rank, never ascending to sobriety, are no longer fit for the higher ranks; but the great masters who are kings of the throne-seat of sobriety, the deputies of the prophets, have attained their desire from this wealth. Luqma — subsistence through God (baqāʾ bi-Llāh) Baqāʾ bi-Llāh means the rank of jamʿ al-jamʿ, which draws on the greatest bewilderment (ḥayrat-i kubrā) — for most of the realized, the final station (though some make contentment and surrender, taslīm o riḍā, the final station). It is named “the return to the beginning” (rujūʿ ilā al-bidāyat; also called baqāʾ baʿd al-fanāʾ, jamʿ al-jamʿ, farq baʿd al-jamʿ, farq-i thānī, ṣaḥw-i thānī; “the end is a return to the beginning”). The “beginning” is the rank of dispersion (tafriqa), where things are apprehended in respect of their determinations and the beginner’s gaze is bound in the phenomena with complete heedlessness. Advancing, the wayfarer attains absence, self-loss, and the perfection of attraction; bonds and determinations are lifted, all individuation effaced. Then he returns to the regard of determinations — but no longer with the initial gaze; his view is now other. Though “the regard of determinations” is common to both ranks (beginning and end), the difference is great and clear: in the first, only determinate, conditioned things are before him, his heart turned to them as Object, with no trace of the Absolute Affair; in the second, his Object is the Absolute Essence alone, his heart turned to none but it, and he sees the determinations as the manifestations of the Names and Attributes. Just as in the first rank he distinguished Majesty and Beauty, so in the second he distinguishes — but now with the other eye. [At the second rank,] some contemplate the creatures by first regarding the Absolute Essence and then, by its light, seeing the determinations; some contemplate the Absolute Essence within things; and some, after contemplating things, contemplate the Absolute Essence. Hence one The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 48

says “I have seen nothing without seeing God before it”; another, “…without seeing God in it”; another, “…without seeing God after it” — each with his appointed station. When the knower reaches the final station (baqāʾ bi-Llāh), it is very hard for common folk to tell him from other people, for his outward is like theirs — whereas the majdhūb and “mad” ones, whose modes are utterly unlike the common, are easily distinguished and revered. This is the station where the holy tradition becomes intelligible: “My saints are beneath My cloak; none knows them but I” (awliyāʾī taḥta qibāʾī lā yaʿrifuhum ghayrī). At this very station some, taunting the Prophet, had said: “What ails this Messenger, that he eats food and walks the markets?” (Q 25:7); and of it God says: “Men whom neither commerce nor trade distracts from the remembrance of God” (Q 24:37). Indeed, among the people of sobriety at the station of the singularity of the Reality (fardiyyat-i ḥaqīqat), the appearance of marvels (khawāriq) is very rare — for their attention is wholly on the pure, colourless Essence, whereas any disposing of the self and the horizons would come through awareness of the effects of the Attributes; the more people are below this station, the more marvels and dispositions appear from them. Its detail is beyond expression, and the verse bears witness: “Say: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before my Lord’s words were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it for replenishment” (Q 18:109). O dear brother! If you study these few lines with the eye of the heart, there is strong hope you will draw yourself up, outwardly, from lowness toward elevation. But I know this work cannot be done without the shaykh’s attention and aid; for in this road are countless perilous, hard-totraverse defiles through which only the shaykh’s inward help can bring one. The study of books is of no use here. You will see certain self-regarding people eager neither to take the pledge (bayʿa) with a shaykh nor to keep the company of any God-reached one, fancying they can perfect dhikr, fikr, and the rest by some book alone — but this is beyond possibility. “Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, for You are the best of deciders” (Q 7:89). The Comprehensive Discourse (Qawl-i Kullī) O seeker of the Real! May God show you His road. Understand this well: of all the kinds of invocations, reflections, and contemplations, the aim of all is one — absorption and annihilation (maḥwiyyat o fanāʾ). In the beginning of its nature, the lordly subtle faculty (laṭīfa-i rabbāniyya) holds the single-pointedness and recollectedness of its resolve; but as connection with creatures grows and worldly attachments multiply, the unity of resolve turns into a multiplicity, until dispersion (tafriqa) replaces recollectedness. The aspiration of the fairminded demands that he turn back toward that unity and mend, by the bond of tawḥīd, the scatteredness in the lordly faculty. There is but one road: to make one’s knowledge simple (basīṭ), abandon the scattered ways, and adopt single-pointedness — until he sees, in all essences the Essence of the Real, in all attributes the Attributes of the Real, in all acts the Acts of the Real. Then this secret dawns: how the Being of the Real pervades the existences of all created things. So adorned with true faith and the perfection of taqwā, it becomes clear to him what Paradise is and what Hell, what this world and the next, what the self is, who Satan and who the Merciful, who the guide and who the misleader — matters that, to the knower, are no object of inquiry, yet by the decree of witnessing (shuhūd) cannot be escaped. In reality, all the methods of invocation, reflection, and contemplation rest on the foundation of love (ʿishq): the greater the love, the greater their effect; the more sluggish the love, the less. By The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 49

persevering in them, the broken thread of love is rejoined and the bond made firm. Invocations should never be done with the intention of gaining merit (thawāb) — the dignity of the lover is far higher than that. Luqma — verses expressing Unity Just as the invocations disclose the meaning of Unity, so in every age verses and poems express these meanings; in the matter of arrival-at-God, they are, like invocations, beneficial. There is this difference: since Arabic has a special relation with the most complete of all manifestations (the Prophet )ﷺ, its effect is greater — though every language’s relation to the prophetic reality is equal, Arabic’s is the stronger. Luqma — the intermediary (barzakh) What the masters appoint as the barzakh is meant to remove scatteredness and gather what is dispersed; by the throng of intrusions a person is left deprived of intellectual Unity (tawḥīd-i ʿilmī), and it is the barzakh that furnishes him with recollectedness of the senses — especially if the barzakh be worthy of reverence, so that the moment the wayfarer sees its form, humility comes over him. By it an intense longing arises for the meanings deposited in that barzakh; for when the imagination is fixed on a thing, it takes on that thing’s colour — its quality being “material” (hayūlānī), with boundless capacity to receive form. As Rūmī says in the Mathnawī: “O brother, you are that very thought; the rest of you is bone and fibre. If in your thought there is a rose, you are a rose-garden; and if a thorn, you are fuel for the furnace.” Anything created can be a barzakh, for barzakh means an intermediary between the heart and the Object — which, by its utmost subtlety, cannot come within apprehension; whatever His beauty is made present in is a barzakh. From the mote to the sun, from the Throne to the floor, every thing is His place of self-display; if the eye is seeing, then whatever you gaze upon, that One is seen. Yet barzakhs differ in rank: the meanings a shaykh bequeaths are quite other than what a pebble can. The subtler and more intellectual the barzakh, the better; the grosser and more merely visible, the more deficient. The masters appoint each wayfarer a barzakh by his capacity — looking to what carries beauty in his eye. If a man loves a youth so that the youth’s beauty outshines the shaykh’s in his eye, it is fitting that the shaykh appoint the youth (not himself) as the barzakh in his exercises, drawing him by this pretext from formal attachment toward meaningful attachment; likewise one who loves flowers above all. By persevering in the exercises he will at last come out of this whirlpool. Reckon the rest by analogy. Luqma — inner heat (ḥarārat-i bāṭinī) Breath-retention, breath-confinement, the two-, four-, and six-stroke dhikr, the Ḥaddādī dhikr, and the like — the aim of all is to produce heat in the inner being. This heat births love and longing; from it fervour arises and the fire of love blazes in the heart. Hence it is said that dhikr shows benefit very quickly in the young, and that “the Sufi grows cold after thirty years.” One does not instruct dhikr in childhood (its heat would burn the child); at puberty it is allowed. The toil possible in youth is not possible in old age, and the vigour and unveiling of early life cannot come late. (Some shaykhs used to bid “cold-blooded” Sufis take certain herbal seeds, that burning and heat might be produced within them.) The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 50

Luqma — the eternal sound (ṣawt-i sarmadī), recapitulated In the foregoing exercises, the heart’s movement, the eternal sound, and the continuous succession of breaths (tawālī-i anfās) have been adopted because their secret is this: these matters, by being the “measure” (miʿyār) of that knowledge which causes nearness and connection, render it perpetually-occurring (dāʾim al-wuqūʿ); since their own perpetuity is established, the thing they measure becomes perpetual too. [As a craftsman alloys gold or silver with a baser metal so the ornament will hold its form, the precious content being the ʿayār and the alloying “standard” the miʿyār — so here the author has made the exercises and invocations the ʿayār, and the heart’s movement and the like the miʿyār.] One might object that within a person too the renewal of likes (tajaddud-i amthāl) runs perpetually — at every instant his “colour” passes away and its like comes anew from non-existence — so why not make that the measure? Answer: first, colours pertain to the eye, whereas in contemplation (and even invocation) closing the eyes is not only useful but necessary; second, this renewal is not self-evident (badīhī) but theoretical (naẓarī), so even a successful proof of it would be merely theoretical. Luqma — the overwhelming of longing (ghalaba-i shawq) The latent melody (naghma) that sleeps in the wayfarer’s nature blazes up from excess of love. At first, weeping, lamentation, and restlessness appear, and trembling and [other] movements proceed from him; fluids flow from eye, nose, and mouth — a condition of pain born of the abundance of dhikr. But those who reach the station of bewilderment do not weep from separation; their weeping is in union — and a difference is told: the tears of those who weep in the very midst of union are sweet, while the tears of those who weep from the pain of separation are salt and bitter. When the people of union (wāṣilīn) dance (raqṣ), their movements are very light, with softness and harmony, mostly to the measure of the melody — this is called the “spiritual resonances” (lawāṭiq-i rūḥānī), evidence of the expansion of the breast (inshirāḥ-i ṣadr) and a momentary joy. Though the common reckon such dance discreditable and gain their expansion from samāʿ by mere excitement, the elite know its wellspring: it is the prostration of the heart (sujūd-i qalb). In an assembly, whoever first rises to dance, and whatever he utters in it, bears the responsibility for whatever colour the assembly then takes — good for good, ill for ill. Sulṭān al-Mashāʾikh [Niẓām al-Dīn] used to say: if a Sufi’s back touches the ground [in ecstasy], he should sacrifice himself or his garment [in thanks]. And Imām al-Qushayrī says: this [ecstatic] movement, from whomever it issues — beginner, intermediate, or advanced — will surely bring some harm to his state; so, until there is an overpowering throng [of ecstasy], let him not stir from his place, but remain, as far as possible, firm and steadfast. Colophon Praise be to God, that this work was brought to completion in the month of Dhū alḤijja, the year 1128 AH. Now, with utmost sincerity and truthfulness of heart, I pray at the court of the Lord of the Worlds: O my Lord! Make this lowly composition of mine accepted by [Your] creatures, and keep it guarded and preserved from the hands of all the [merely worldly] people of existence and the fault-finding carpers. And I ask too that, by the grace of Your pure Beloved — the master of the righteous The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 51

and the most pure — [You bless him]; may God bless and give peace to the Messenger, the best of His creation, Muḥammad, and his family. Āmīn! — َتَّم ْت ِباْلَخ ْیِرTammat bi’l-khayr — Completed with good. The Kashkūl-i Kalīmī — Telegram: @DhikrNotes Page 52

Foreword Much time has passed since Professor Dr Mir Valiuddin submitted his manuscript to the Press. He did not live to see it printed, for he passed away in 1975, when the last touches were given to the manuscript. Since the publisher intended to make the contents available to a great number of non-specialists it was deemed necessary to cut out the copious Arabic, Persian, and Urdu quotations, to print which would have caused much difficulty. Since the number of people in the West who are seriously interested in the problems of Sufism has increased considerably during the last decade we felt that they should not be deprived of the contents of Dr Valiuddin’s work due to the language barrier. This was also the reason why the style was sometimes changed, repetitions, as are almost unavoidable, were cut out, so that the book can now be used easily by all those who are interested in the spiritual techniques of Sufism. Dr. Gulshan Khakee, herself trained in the discipline of Comparative Religions and conversant with both the Muslim and the Hindu traditions, has edited the manuscript carefully, and added a bibliography which may help the readers in their further research. The material that has been assembled here has never before been offered to a larger audience of Western readers, and it is to be hoped that it will stimulate a deeper interest in the practices of classical Sufism and also incite scholars to enter more deeply into the field of scholarly study of mystical techniques and their influence on the human mind. Dr. Annemarie Schimmel Professor of Indo-Muslim Culture Harvard University May 1979

Preface Dr Mir Valiuddin, who died in 1975, has already made valuable contributions to authentic Sufi literature in English through his books, especially The Quranic Sufism (Delhi, 1959) and Love of God, The Sufi Approach (Delhi, 1968), and through many articles that have appeared in various journals during the past thirty years. With the present study he makes an important contribution to an aspect of Sufism which has received little attention until now. The official Orientalists, unaware for the most part of the techniques and methods of Sufism, have been in no position to make a meaningful study of spiritual techniques the like of which were lost in the West a long time ago and only now are being avidly sought after in the Eastern Traditions. As for the occultists and pseudo-spiritualists, whose number increases every day with the weakening of the spiritual forces in the West, they have spoken of spiritual techniques and in fact have of late invaded the field of Sufism after adulterating for some time Hinduism and Buddhism. But because they are not traditional and orthodox in the true sense of these words—and have no respect for the Sacred Law or Sharia, which alone can make possible even the first step upon the Path—they speak in a vacuum. They offer techniques of meditation and contemplation which at best may be of only minor harm and at worst can lead men into madness and demonic states of consciousness. It is, therefore, especially welcome that the present book is devoted to Sufi disciplines from the point of view of Sufism itself and presented by one who has spent a life-time in their study and practice, one who is immersed in these disciplines himself. The exposition of the author is the fruit of the long tradition of Sufism as it has existed over the centuries and as it has manifested itself in the Arabic, Persian and Urdu literatures. The pages of the

viii CONTEMPLATIVE DISCIPLINES IN SUFISM book are replete with quotations from the rich poetry of all of these languages, especially Persian, which for centuries was as much a cultural language of the Indian sub-continent as of Persia itself. The beauty of the book lies most of all in the well-chosen verses —some of celestial beauty — which can be fully appreciated only in the original. It is understandable that in this book, for several reasons, only the translations into English of these verses can be given. The very rich selection presented in these pages demonstrates the author's immense learning and his close acquaintance with Sufism and its literature in the several languages mentioned above. The vast number of citations which have been abridged in this edited edition of the original manuscript for economic reasons, also demonstrates the organic link which exists between the Koran and Hadith and early Sufi Poetry in Arabic and the vast treasures of Persian and later Urdu Sufi poetry. These mystical literatures are like so many streams which flow forth from the gushing spring of inspiration deriving from the Holy Koran. The great virtue of this book is in fact to start by ascertaining categorically the Koranic origin of Sufism.' To have shown that the practice of Sufism is essentially the emulation of the life and practice of the Holy Prophet and its goal the true knowledge or ma ‘ifa of the message of the Holy Koran that can be summarized in the majestic quintessence of all metaphysics, namely, La tlaha iil Allah is already to have rendered a great service to the cause of Islam and to Sufism. For this affirmation will at least keep away the would-be pretender who, not being serious enough to accept the discipline implied in the Shari‘ of Islam, wishes to practise Sufism as an extraneous element that has been grafted on to the body of Islam and has somehow survived to modern times just awaiting occultists who, thinking that they know Sufism better than the Sufis themselves, can plunder its riches. The long introduction to the book, replete with quotations from leading authorities of Sufism throughout the ages, makes clear the meaning of Sufism, its relation to the Sharé‘a, the position of some of the great intellectual figures of Islam towards it, and the reason for the opposition of some of the very esoteric elements in Islamic society against it. In the eight chapters that follow, the author outlines the stages of the spiritual path (suluk), which consist essentially of the purification of different levels of the microcosmic being, the nafs, the galb and the sirr, and finally the illumination of the spirit by Divine Light

PREFACE ix resulting in the gnosis which is the end and goal of the Sufi path. Moreover, the stages of the Path are delineated according to the teachings of the three major Sufi orders of the sub-continent: the Qadiriyya, the Naqshbandiyya and the Chistiyya. The description of the fundamental technique of invocation (dhskr) with numerous citations from Sufi texts in both prose and poetry remains central throughout these chapters. Of particular interest is the description of the silent invocation of the Naqshbandiyya. The author states clearly his preference for the ‘way of love’ of the Chishtiyya, following what he has expressed in his previous works. It must be made clear, however, that the love stressed here should not be confused with the ‘way of love’ known to the post-medieval West, which is usually seen as separated or even opposed to the way of knowledge. In Islam love and knowledge can never be totally separated. Each Sufi order only stresses one without ever denying the other. In fact Sufi love (‘tshq) is understood by Sufis as the realized aspect of gnosis. The purest metaphysics, if it remains only theoretical, is little as compared with its realization in the soul of man. This realization is called ‘ishq#, it is a love that is wedded to gnosis and leads to Unity or tawhid, which is situated above all duality, even the duality existing between the lover and the Beloved. That is why the ‘poet of the Invisible World’ (lisan al-ghayb) Hafiz writes: The men of intellect (those who possess theoretical knowledge) are like the central point of the compass of existence. But Love (‘ishq) knows that they are lost wandering in this circle. The exposition of Dr Valiuddin has the virtue of both depicting the contours of this circle of existence and indicating how through the stages of spiritual realization man can reach that realized gnosis which sees every formulation as but a key to the understanding of the Truth which in essence is infallible and remains above all formulations. Introduction In the following pages an attempt has been made to enunciate the contemplative disciplines in Sufism as practised by the great Sufis and eminent Shaykhs. But before we proceed to do this, let us understand the exalted position that the Sufis occupy in the community of the Muslims—‘men chosen and elect, excellent and pre-eminent’. As Abu Bakr al-Kalabadhi' has said about them: Their feet were firm, their understandings clean, their beacons were bright: they had understanding of God, and journeyed unto God, and turned away from what is other than God. Their lights pierced the veils . . . and their eyes were blind to all beneath the Throne. They were spiritual bodies . . . silent and meditative, absent from men but present with God, kings in Tags . . . possessors of all virtues and lights of all guidance; their ears attentive, their hearts pure, their qualities concealed; chosen, illuminated, pure. Abu Yazid said: The Sufis are children in the lap of God. Yusuf ibn al-Husayn said: There is in every community a chosen band, and they are the agents of God, concealed by Him from His creation; if there be any such in this community, they are the Sufis. Dhu'n-Nun’ said: I saw a woman in one of the coasts of Syria and said to her, “Whence comest thou (God have mercy on thee)?’ She replied, ‘From people whose flanks shrink from beds.’ I said, ‘And whither intendest thou?’ She answered, ‘Unto them whom neither merchandise, nor selling diverts from remembrance said, ‘Describe them.’ of God’? I

xii CONTEMPLATIVE DISCIPLINES IN SUFISM Then she began to recite: Their every purpose is with God united, Their high ambitions mount to Him alone: Their troth is to the Lord and Master plighted — O noble quest, for the Eternal One! They do not quarrel over this world’s pleasure — Honours, and children, rich and costly gowns, All greed and appetite! They do not treasure The life of ease and joy that dwells in towns. Facing the far and faint horizon yonder They seek the Infinite, with purpose strong: They ever tread where desert runnels wander, And high on towering mountain-tops they throng!‘ Perhaps this will suffice to give an idea of the high rank of the Sufis in the Muslim community. Now let us record a few of the Traditions of the Prophet of Islam about Sufism. Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyib relates, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet said: Verily, a part of knowledge is after something hidden; it is only known by those who are acquainted with God. When they speak about it, it is disapproved of by those who are heedless of God. The following narrative goes back to ‘Abd al-Wahid ibn Zayd: I asked al-Hasan about the science of the Inward, and hé said, ‘I asked Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman about the science of the Inward, and he said, “I asked the Messenger of God about the science of the Inward, and he said ‘I asked Gabriel about the science of the Inward, and he said, “I asked God about the science of the Inward, and He said, ‘It is a secret of My secrets; I set it in the heart of my servant, and none of My creatures understands it.’ ** Abu 11-Hasan ibn Abi Dharr quotes the following verses of al-Shibli in his book, the Minhaj ad-Din: The science of the Sufis has no bound, Ascience high, celestial, divine: In it the Masters have plunged profound, And men of wit appraise them by that sign. We will amplify the statements made above in order to understand the position of the Sufis and the nature and value of their teachings. ‘Allama Qutb ad-Din Shirazi‘ has given a true picture of the Sufis

INTRODUCTION xiii and their work. He says that the Messenger of God (God's blessings and peace be upon him) has said: The ‘ulama (the learned class) of my people are like the prophets of the sons of Israel. This means that the ‘ulama of the Muslim community are like the prophets of the sons of Israel in knowing the path to God and leading men towards it. He has also said: The ‘ulama are the heirs to the prophets. The heritage of the prophets is the Proximity of God. Attainment unto God is possible, firstly, by acquiring the knowledge imparted by the Shari'a (sacred law). This knowledge teaches us how to discharge the obligations imposed upon us in connection with the service, worship and adoration of God and also in relation to our fellow beings. When we discharge our duties in strict accordance with the dictates of the Shari'a, we are led on the way to attainment unto God which ultimately leads us to the spring whence those brought near to God drink.’ In the same way, ‘Proximity to God’ is attained by acquiring the knowledge of the ‘Path of God’, %lm at-Tariqa. It teaches us to cultivate that mental state which is the result of the attainment of angelic qualities, and of the purification of the appetitive self from its blamable animal attributes and purging it of its depravity, and of the cleansing of the heart from the love of the ephemeral world, from its leaning towards the worldlings and its vainglorious thoughts and making it the object of Divine Effulgence. In this way heart and soul and self are prepared for the attainment unto God. Again, the ‘Proximity of God’ is attained by acquiring the ‘im alHaqiqa, ‘knowledge of the Truth’. It consists of the gnosis of the Names and Attributes of God° and teaches us how to actualize or realize them in ourselves. ‘Gnosis’ in the words of Faris ‘absorbs the gnostic in the essence of the Object of his gnosis’. Thus, according to Shirazi, the Sufi shaykhs tread on the paths of Shari‘a (the Sacred Law), Tariga (the Path) and Hagiqa (the Truth) and they establish true relationship with the Prophets by their knowledge, words, deeds and ahwal or ‘mystic states’. This is not done by the formalists among the ‘ulama, the ‘learned class’. Another eminent scholar, who is considered among those ‘who are firmly grounded in knowledge’, ‘Allama Jalal ad-Din Dawwani, says in his Sharh-i Ruba tyat:

xiv CONTEMPLATIVE DISCIPLINES IN SUFISM Formal sciences do not lead us to Reality; but that which directs us to it is, after Divine blessing, the company of, or intimate association with the “inward” men of the Path and devotion to these ecstatics. Though the methods of argumentation or reasoning resolve many difficulties and remove many obstacles, those who aspire after Reality find no peace or bliss by these methods. As the great Sufi alHallaj has said: Who seeks God, and takes the intellect for guide, God drives him forth, in vain distraction to abide: With wild confusion He confounds his inmost heart, So that, distraught, he cries, ‘I know not if Thou art’. '° This can be seen from the writings of some of those great scholars who were first engaged in the study of formal sciences and spent a great part of their life in argumentation, methodical reasoning and debate, but could not achieve their goal. So they left this way of seeking Reality and took to seclusion, privacy and avoidance of intercourse with people. Such was Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazzali (d. 1111)'' who has related his own story in his book al-Mungidh min ad-Dalal and other works. Similarly, Hamadhani has dwelt on this subject in Zubdat al- Haqa ‘tq where he says: For the seeker of the purification of the inward, the society of and association with men of direct intuitive knowledge is of immense value. By men of direct intuitive knowledge I mean those singular men who have purified their hearts from all vices and to whom the benignity and grace of God reveal things that cannot be described in words. The felicity of the seeker lies in the devoted services of those saints who are dead to themselves and entirely lost in God, becoming one spirit with Him in all respects. When they thus spent their lives in ardent love of God and devoted service to Him, God grants them a sweet, clean, happy, good life. The learned men of the formalist type know nothing except the outward form or impress of Reality. If you desire to realise Truth: Refrain from debates and discussions as genuine seekers do. Keep company with Friends of God and mingle with them, May be that you soar high with their wings. And again: We indulged in academic discussions endless, But failed to solve the mysteries of the universe.

INTRODUCTION xv Though several knots have been disentangled, Nothing is known about the Hereafter! The eminent Shaykh ‘Abd al-Wahab Sha‘rani writes in his work Irshad at - Talabah wal-Muridin: One should know that the Way of the Sufis is the only straight way, the clear and upright way. Ways are sought for the advantages gained in following them, and the way of the Sufis is the way of the exact gnosis of God, and of knowledge of the diverse ways of self training necessary for the gnosis of God. And everybody knows that the gnosis of God is the highest and the noblest of all knowledge, because the object of this knowledge is the Most Excellent Being. That is why the way of gnosis of God is the most excellent of all ways and one who guides us towards this end is the master of all guides and the most perfect of them all. And the traveller of this path is the most blessed of all travellers . . . Hence, one who would like to admonish or give good counsel to his own self should follow this path only, giving up all other paths. For this is the path of felicity and bliss which comprises of both the sciences of Shari'a and Tariga. The gnostic of this path is the perfect adept and the true heir to the Inheritance of the Prophets. He is called the Universal Man or the Perfect Master. Further, it should be noted that as the stage attained by following this path is the most excellent and felicitous one, the path itself is hard to travel, being replete with trials and tribulations; and one who treads this path is really a brave man who holds the hand of his spiritual preceptor firmly and marches on boldly towards the ultimate end. It is incumbent on the preceptor to pay due attention to the training of the disciple, and it is incumbent on the disciple to follow the instructions of his preceptor whole-heartedly. The eminent Shaykh Muhammad ibn Mahmud Bukhari, known as Khwaja Parsa Nagshbandi says: The Shaykhs of the Tariga (‘path’) are the leaders of all men of true religion and belief. They have acquired for themselves all the inward and outward aspects of knowledge. They are men of feeling (arbab-i ahwal) and perfect masters. Their beliefs are based on true principles and are supported by the Holy Koran, the Traditions of the Prophet, the agreement of all Muslims and rational arguments. They are also ahl-t dil ‘men of heart’, inward men who look through the veil. God Almighty has turned towards

xvi CONTEMPLATIVE DISCIPLINES IN SUFISM them with benignty and sufficient Grace and has attracted them towards Himself and for whom ‘the good (record) from us has gone before’ and ‘made them stick close to the command of self restraint, and well were they entitled to it and worthy of it’. They have received their knowledge from God, and have devoted themselves to His service alone, to the complete exclusion of all else, their light has torn asunder all the veils and their hearts have moved around the Throne of God. They are men of inflexible purpose, stout of heart, elect among the believers. They are a light for the seekers of God. They exterminate false pretensions and innovations; they are proof as it were for the people of the ahl-i Sunna or the ‘approved way’. God in His wisdom and Mercy has revealed the light of their saintship among the believers so that they may be blessed and benefit by them. For such God has written faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Himself.'’ Those who oppose them are spiritually dead as they do not perceive. Imam Ghazzali,'* in his work al-Mungidh min ad-Dalal, after mentioning the early stages of his life, says: Many secrets and mysteries have been revealed to me in these seclusions and privacy with God which cannot be recounted here. I shall relate only those which I think may benefit the readers of this treatise. With a heartfelt certainty I came to believe that the eminent Sufis alone are the veracious travellers on the Path of God and their disposition, manners and habits alone are superior to all others. Their way alone is the straight way. Their natural disposition and morals are the best . . . This is so because all their outward actions and inward states are irradiated by the light of the lamp of prophecy, and there is not on the face of the earth any other light from which illumination should be sought. In short the very first condition of this Holy way is the overcoming of the appetites of the flesh and getting rid of its evil dispositions and vile qualities, so that the heart may be cleared of all but God; and the means of clearing it is dhikr-e Allah, i.e. the commemoration of God and concentration of every thought upon Him. And the last stage of this way is complete effacement in God —the naughting of all that is not God and persisting through what belongs to God. Who can find fault with such a way? That which we have described as the last stage of Sufism is not really the last one. It is last in the sense that what is achieved by painfully treading the via purgativa by self remonstrance and self abnegation is this stage. As a matter of fact, this is only the first stage of the Path to God. What proceeded before this stage was only a threshold for the seeker. It is a way in which in its very first stage mukashafas or ‘unveilings’ come to the disciples; while

'‘ Then their hal ‘state’ passes from the beholding of forms to stages where language fails and any attempt to express what is experienced must involve some error. They reach a proximity to God which some have fancied to be hulul, ‘fusion of being’, others ztt¢had ‘identification’ and others wusul or ‘union’. But all these are erroneous ways of indicating the thing. In our book al-maqsad al-Aqsa we have explained where the error lies... Unless a man has felt in himself some part of this matter z.e. of the highest mystical states, he knows nothing of Prophecy as it really is, except the name. The miraculous gifts of the Sufi saints are the first things that happen to the Prophets. Such was the case with Muhammad, (may the peace of God be upon him) at the outset, when he retired to Mount Hira to be alone with God and gave himself up to devotion. At this the Arabs began to whisper among themselves that Muhammad had fallen in love with his Lord. This is the state which is known only to those men of taste and ecstacy, the ahl-i dhauq who have traversed the path. Those who have not experienced this joy may come to know of it Ly experience or from hearing about it from the ‘men of feeling’. And this is possible only when they associate with them for a long time. He who keeps company with these people will attain to this state and faith. Those to whom this bliss of personal experience has not been granted may believe in it through rational proof or ‘demonstration’ burhan, as we have shown in our book Thya ‘Ulum ad-Din, in the chapter on ‘Aja%b al-Qulub or ‘Mysteries of the Heart’. To describe this mystic state in words and support it by arguments and proof is called knowledge, to acquire it by experience and practice is called dhaug (‘taste’) and to form an opinion about it and believe it implicitly is faith. These are the three stages. As the Koran says: God will raise up to suitable ranks (and degrees) those of you who believe and who have been granted (mystic) knowledge. '* As opposed to them are the ignorant people who do not know it and therefore deny and disavow it. It is about them that the Koran has said And among them are men who listen to thee, but in the end when they go out from thee, they say to those who have received

Shaykh Dia ad-Din Abu Najib Suhrawardi (d. 1168) in his book Adab al-Muridin says: . . .
